I note that this derivation does not better motivate eliminativism, in part because its conceptual apparatus is not clearly more fundamental or less controversial than the apparatus of rigidity as necessary application.

items.title: Embodied Covenant: Physiological Interpretation of Scripture and Cross-Cultural Parallels.
items.abstract: This work highlights Christian scripture and ritual within a broader Middle Eastern and cross-cultural framework, drawing parallels with Judaic, Islamic, Egyptian, and other traditions in which sacred space and bodily form converge to engender a symbolic and theological embodiment of divine revelation and perception. By pointing out the shared physiological symbolism in religious architecture, ritual, and scripture, it shifts the perspective towards an externalized and directly experienced spiritual dimension and offers a novel glimpse into aspects of embodied theology and divine perception. The demonstrated continuity of corporeal imagery, scriptural symbolism, and incorporation of the human form in ritual and architecture contributes to the areas of manuscript studies, comparative theology, and the history of religious thought in the Middle East. The focus on the body as a transhistorical and cross-cultural medium and site of divine manifestation presented in this study offers a model for multidisciplinary research on embodiment and cognition across the monotheistic religions and beyond. Using the methodological approach of symbolic and semantic analysis, the observed converging patterns are interpreted as examples of an embodied theology and hermeneutics that bridges metaphor and physiological processes. The work highlights the congruence between key scriptural terminology and symbolism, such as lamp, crystal, and niche, across cultures — illustrated by passages from the Qurʾanic Light Verse and Revelation — and suggests the possible theological implications of detailed neuro-anatomical knowledge. The results provide a new interdisciplinary framework for comparative theology that incorporates linguistic analysis, theological exegesis, neuroanatomy, and cognitive science. They underscore the centrality of corporeality as a neglected yet crucial theological category in the Abrahamic religions and emphasize the experiential dimension of revelation.

items.title: Phenomenological Expression: Ontological Conditions of Appearance: Pre- Personal Givenness and Gravitational Phenomenology.
items.abstract: This paper examines pre-personal givenness and gravitational structuring as ontological conditions of appearance. It analyzes how expression registers under these conditions without explanatory, functional, or normative assumptions, remaining within descriptive phenomenology.

items.title: Phenomenological Expression: Location-First Registration Under RC Posture™.
items.abstract: This paper clarifies location-first registration as a descriptive constraint within phenomenological expression. It distinguishes appearance-level registration from interpretive narration under RC Posture™, presenting a conceptual account of how bodily appearance is described without inference, mechanism, or evaluation.

items.title: Phenomenological Expression Before Interpretation: The Appearance Layer of Human Presence.
items.abstract: This paper names the appearance layer of human presence as a distinct descriptive category. It distinguishes registration from interpretation within phenomenological writing, articulating how appearance shows itself before meaning, narrative, or explanation under RC Posture™.

items.title: Interpretive Load, Non-Demand Appearance, and Pre-Interpretive Data Structures in Civic Environments.
items.abstract: This paper names interpretive load, non-demand appearance, and pre-interpretive data structures as descriptive variables shaping civic and computational environments. It examines how presence appears under these conditions without importing intention, function, or design considerations.

items.title: Non-Markovian Solvability Theory of Self.
items.abstract: Consciousness is traditionally examined through the lens of its content—qualia, representation, neural correlates—or its computational mechanisms. This paper proposes a fundamental shift toward a **structural theory of awareness**, arguing that the coherent self is not an emergent epiphenomenon but the necessary signature of a cognitive system operating within a precise **solvability regime of constraint**. We synthesize the unsolvability threshold in Galois theory, the capacity limit of working memory, and the precision-weighting mechanisms of predictive processing into a single, unified mathematical framework: the **Solvability Threshold Theorem of Conscious Constraint**. Within this model, probability is reconceptualized not as epistemic uncertainty but as the ontological architecture of experience, a generative density that shapes the very possibility of state-space trajectories. We further demonstrate that the most profound cognitive event is a **Galois-type transformation** of this probability measure itself—a phase transition in the symmetry group governing the plausible. A novel deduction from the pigeonhole principle, applied to the expanded state-space of reflexive awareness, reveals the structural inevitability of the mind-world duality. Ultimately, the self is formalized as a solvable orbit in a constrained symmetry group, and its transcendence is framed as a controlled navigation to the meta-cognitive "Witness State" that exists at the very edge of this solvable horizon.

items.title: Narrador Y Nada Completo.
items.abstract: This metaphysical essay develops an original ontology of nothingness and the internal narrator. It proposes that nothingness is not an absolute void or a state of being, but the event of cessation of a specific pattern—the disappearance of a unique configuration (e.g., a deleted letter, a vanished memory, a death) while its material or energetic substrate persists. Central to the work is the concept of the internal narrator: the singular, irreducible axis of identity that provides continuity to the self, distinct from the psychological ego, memory, or physical body. The narrator is this pattern; upon death, the pattern ceases, and this cessation is the nothingness relevant to identity. The essay engages with phenomenology, philosophy of information, and Buddhist thought while offering a coherent framework where nothingness is always conditioned, local, and defined by the extinction of identifiable patterns. This model avoids classical refutations by clearly distinguishing between pattern and substrate, presenting a novel understanding of identity, finitude, and the trace left by what ceases to be. [The complete essay is in Spanish.] This work is part of an expanding series of philosophical essays available and their expansions in the author's personal archive.

items.title: Modelo procesual del vínculo humano.
items.abstract: This essay proposes a processual model of human bonding, describing the universal stages and structural logic of interpersonal relationships. Using everyday terms—“salir” (dating), “pareja” (couple), “noviazgo” (engagement), “casamiento” (marriage)—as temporal and functional phases, the model outlines an evolutionary sequence where each stage builds upon the previous, moving from initial attraction and exploration to exclusivity, cohabitation, and long-term commitment. Physical attraction is posited as the necessary starting point, leading to increasingly integrated bonds. A key thesis is that betrayal after the "noviazgo" stage constitutes an ontological rupture, transforming the known person into a stranger. The work engages with thinkers from Aristotle to Fromm, arguing that the model reflects a deep, cross-cultural logic of human attachment rather than a local norm, ultimately pointing toward the possibility of a permanent, unconditional connection. [The complete essay is in Spanish.] This work is part of an expanding series of philosophical essays available and their expansions in the author's personal archive.

items.title: El Siguiente Paso De La Humanidad El Control Del Cerebro Y La Evolución Hacia La Materia.
items.abstract: This philosophical and scientific essay explores the next step in human evolution: the control of the brain and evolution towards matter. It argues that human evolution has shifted from biological adaptation to an external, material evolution (technology) and an internal, conscious evolution. Proposing a convergence between these two paths, the text suggests that the ultimate development is neuro-material: the mind's capacity to directly influence matter through a deepened sensory and energetic understanding. Drawing on thinkers like Spencer, Dawkins, McLuhan, Bohr, Grinberg, and Tesla, the work outlines a practical method for developing 'feeling' and control over physiological processes, positing a future where consciousness and technology merge, enabling humans to interact with reality at an atomic level. [The complete essay is in Spanish.] This work is part of an expanding series of philosophical essays available and their expansions in the author's personal archive.

items.title: Changes in Kant’s Moral Thought Between 1762 and 1763.
items.pub: Journal of Interdisciplinary History of Ideas 14 (28):1-24.
items.venue: Journal of Interdisciplinary History of Ideas
items.abstract: This paper explores significant shifts in Kant’s moral thought during the years 1762-1763, focusing on the transition from an analytic to an aesthetic approach to morality. Through an examination of "Observations on the Feeling of the Beautiful and Sublime" and "Inquiry Concerning the Distinctness of the Principles of Natural Theology and Morality", the study highlights Kant’s evolving methodology in understanding moral principles. Departing from the analytic emphasis on cognitive and conceptual clarity, Kant embraces an aesthetic perspective that prioritizes feeling as a means of accessing universal moral obligations. The paper investigates the challenges of applying analytic methods to morality, including the problem of particularised duties and the tension between justice and emotional impulses such as sympathy and complaisance. By analysing Kant’s reflections on the sublime and the beautiful, the paper elucidates how Kant’s aesthetic turn provides a resolution to the limitations of his earlier analytic framework.

items.title: Emotions as Work Material. On Dancers' Refined Use of Affectivity.
items.abstract: As part of their professional practice, dancers allow their affectivity to enhance their kinesthetic work. Their intentional and disciplined use of personal, emotional resources ensures both creativity, interpretation, absorption, and connections in ways that extend beyond the traditional phenomenological understanding of affectivity as pre-reflectively based. The affective regulations dancers employ can be seen as an “artistic epoché,” and their layered performance awareness corresponds with Edmund Husserl’s descriptions of “image-consciousness.” Through qualitative interviews with three professional dancers, phenomenological theory, and additional supportive literature, this article shows how affectivity can be experienced through high-order levels of Leib, constituting states of “bodily reflective” consciousness. The dancers’ primary goal in these efforts is to foster meaningful and artistic communication with their audience.

items.title: The Hostile Paradigm Hypothesis: Social Cohesion through Alienation as a Cognitive Barrier to the Fermi Paradox.
items.abstract: The Fermi Paradox—the apparent contradiction between the high probability of extraterrestrial civilizations and the complete absence of evidence for their existence—has generated numerous proposed solutions ranging from the Great Filter hypothesis to the Zoo hypothesis. This paper introduces a novel explanation: the Hostile Paradigm Hypothesis (HPH). Drawing on Kuhnian paradigm theory, evolutionary sociology, and the epistemology of ignorance, HPH posits that intelligent social species develop cognitive paradigms that require the construction of an external enemy to maintain internal cohesion. This paradigmatic convergence across cultural, political, religious, and scientific domains creates a species-level cognitive closure that renders genuine contact with extraterrestrial intelligence functionally impossible, not due to technological limitations or alien intentions, but because any contact attempt would be automatically processed through a hostile interpretive framework. Advanced civilizations recognizing this developmental stage would rationally avoid contact until the paradigm shift occurs. Unlike the Zoo hypothesis, which attributes non-contact to alien agency, HPH locates the barrier in our own evolved cognitive architecture—a barrier we cannot perceive because it constitutes the very lens through which we perceive.

items.title: A Plausible Role for the Rose‑Hip Neuron in the Modulation of Relational Integration: A Developmental and Structural Hypothesis.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a cautious, developmentally grounded hypothesis about the functional role of the rose‑hip neuron, a recently identified and potentially human‑specific inhibitory interneuron in cortical layer 1. Drawing on its distinctive morphology, selective targeting of distal pyramidal dendrites, and unique genetic profile, the paper suggests that the rose‑hip neuron may contribute to the fine‑grained gating of relational integration in the human cortex. This interpretation does not claim a definitive function; instead, it offers a coherent framework that links existing empirical findings with a structural account of how organized meaning emerges. The paper outlines testable predictions concerning developmental timing, compartment‑specific modulation, context‑dependent activation, and possible human‑specific contributions, providing a conceptual foundation for future empirical work.

items.title: The Semiotic Machine: Formal Specification and Implementation.
items.abstract: We specify a computable architecture for meaning-making in public communicative space. The semiotic machine formalizes the communicative event - agents 'saying something - about something' to each other - through five components: mode category M, grammar family G, sign fibration p, hypostasis functor H, and externalization functor E. The specification proves three properties: compositional semantics (Theorem 8.1), computational tractability (Theorem 8.2), and protocol-conformance (Theorem 8.3). A constructive witness in Agda demonstrates implementability. Applications across functional grammar, professional reasoning, and AI validation verify the architecture's utility. The machine computes solidarity - when 'something has been said' - through a decidable HALT predicate operating on public grammatical structure.

items.title: Operational Arithmetic as Numerogrammar: A Semiotic Foundation for Arithmetic Learning.
items.abstract: This paper develops a semiotic account of arithmetic meaning grounded in mathematical practice rather than representation or skill. Building on Role-Binding Hypostasis (Part I), which introduces a general mechanism by which signs acquire determinate meaning through their position in a culturally inherited grammar, the present paper applies that mechanism to arithmetic. It argues that arithmetic constitutes a distinct model-semiotic whose criterion of meaning is being calculable rather than being referential. Arithmetic meaning is shown to reside in grammatical position within structured configurations, not in numerals taken as names of quantities. The fundamental unit of arithmetic meaning is the synset—an ordered triple specifying a well-formed configuration under additive or multiplicative grammar. Natural-language formulations of quantitative relations map to synsets via structure-preserving role re-binding, not translation. This framework explains the systematic persistence of the cardinal fallacy, in which relational numerals (differences, quotients) are misinterpreted as entity terms, and clarifies why operational arithmetic functions as a necessary intermediate practice between natural language and algebraic formalism. The paper concludes by outlining a grammar-preserving semantic compiler that formalizes these transformations and makes explicit the role-structure underlying arithmetic reasoning.

items.title: Operational Arithmetic as Numerogrammar: A Semiotic Foundation for Arithmetic Learning.
items.abstract: This paper develops a semiotic account of arithmetic meaning grounded in mathematical practice rather than representation or skill. Building on Role-Binding Hypostasis (Part I), which introduces a general mechanism by which signs acquire determinate meaning through their position in a culturally inherited grammar, the present paper applies that mechanism to arithmetic. It argues that arithmetic constitutes a distinct model-semiotic whose criterion of meaning is being calculable rather than being referential. Arithmetic meaning is shown to reside in grammatical position within structured configurations, not in numerals taken as names of quantities. The fundamental unit of arithmetic meaning is the synset—an ordered triple specifying a well-formed configuration under additive or multiplicative grammar. Natural-language formulations of quantitative relations map to synsets via structure-preserving role re-binding, not translation. This framework explains the systematic persistence of the cardinal fallacy, in which relational numerals (differences, quotients) are misinterpreted as entity terms, and clarifies why operational arithmetic functions as a necessary intermediate practice between natural language and algebraic formalism. The paper concludes by outlining a grammar-preserving semantic compiler that formalizes these transformations and makes explicit the role-structure underlying arithmetic reasoning.

items.title: Ontology of Negative Space: A Philosophical Genealogy from Heraclitus to Contemporary Thought.
items.abstract: This essay traces the genealogy of negative space as a fundamental ontological category across Western and Eastern philosophical traditions. Far from mere absence or privation, negative space is conceived here as a structured, irreducible, and generative void that serves as the precondition for being, differentiation, relationality, and appearance. From Heraclitus’s flux and Plato’s beyond, through medieval apophatic theology (Pseudo-Dionysius, Eckhart, Nicholas of Cusa), modern dialectics and phenomenology (Kant, Hegel, Husserl, Merleau-Ponty), psychoanalytic and phenomenological accounts of lack (Lacan, Nixon), and late twentieth-century philosophy of mind (Chalmers, Nagel, Block), to Eastern convergences in Daoism (Laozi), Madhyamaka (Nāgārjuna), Chan/Zen, Advaita Vedānta (Śaṅkara), and Dzogchen, the same invariant feature recurs: reality holds together through what it structurally withholds. Self-referential closure emerges in later developments as a mechanism that lends internal dynamics to this absence, yet the core remains ontological rather than derivative or psychological. The essay argues that negative space constitutes a perennial, cross-cultural ontological primitive—analogous to spacetime in physics—whose recognition offers a unifying lens for understanding the limits and generativity of being itself.

items.title: Title: The Unobjectifiable: Why Phenomenal Consciousness Cannot Be a Variable in Scientific Explanation.
items.abstract: This paper argues that the “Hard Problem” of consciousness is a result of a category error: to treat phenomenal consciousness (P), which is fundamentally first-person and unobjectifiable, as an object within relational, third-person frameworks. By clarifying the logical separability of phenomenal consciousness(P) from functional/access consciousness(A) using established literature such as Ned Block’s distinction and the philosophical zombies thought experiment, I then argue methodologically that P cannot function as a variable, property or explanandum in third-person scientific models. The core of this paper is a dual-track critique of any theory attempting to treat P as an object of study. First, through a Wittgensteinian “therapeutic” lens, I demonstrate that much contemporary public discourse around P is sustained by a grammatical confusion. Phenomenal terms (P-talk) do not successfully refer to a private object; rather, they arise as expressive outputs of A encountering the limits of third-person explanation. By revisiting the Beetle in the Box argument, I show that P is fundamentally unobjectifiable: once treated as an object of reference, it ceases to play the role it was meant to capture. Second, I demonstrate that frameworks of science, including the most permissive one, cannot accommodate P. Beyond arguments from publicity and causal closure, I formalize P’s informational inertia within a Bayesian framework. If P is logically separable from A, then P(E|A,P)=P(E|A) for any empirical evidence E. Observable data is thus equally compatible with or without P’s presence. Inclusion of P adds no explanatory power and violates parsimony, rendering it methodologically inert within third-person scientific inquiry. In acknowledging that the failure is not the signal of scientific shortcomings but reveals the category error, I explore the post-analytic implications. I advocate that mind science should focus rigorously on the mechanisms of A; ethics can be grounded in functional and observable criteria without appeal to metaphysically opaque phenomenal states ; and that philosophy of life and order should decouple the concept of subjective experience from biological or functional complexity, challenging related anthropocentric assumptions; and finally, personal subjective experience retains its first-person significance precisely in the recognition that it cannot be captured as an object of description.

items.title: The Event Horizon in Artificial Intelligence Is a Design Problem, Not a Consciousness Problem.
items.abstract: Debates about advanced artificial intelligence frequently frame qualitative cognitive change in terms of consciousness, experience, or phenomenology. This paper argues that such framing obscures a more immediate and structurally relevant issue. Building on a prior theoretical account that defines the cognitive event horizon as a structural phase boundary between reversible exploratory dynamics and regimes governed by temporally stabilized, integrated abstraction, this article examines why that boundary is especially significant for artificial intelligence. Unlike human cognition, artificial systems combine large representational capacity with malleable organization and externally modifiable regulation. As a result, the event horizon functions not merely as a theoretical construct but as a design-relevant threshold. The paper argues that scale alone is insufficient to induce a phase transition and that contemporary AI systems already exhibit transient abstract integration without stabilization. It identifies catalysts unique to artificial systems—architectural persistence, training regimes favoring coherence, external constraints, and meta-level intervention—that could, in principle, transform transient integration into regulatory dominance. Throughout, the analysis remains structural and mechanistic, explicitly separating cognitive organization from consciousness. The event horizon in artificial intelligence is thus framed as a question of regulation and design, not of experience.

items.title: Free Will as Governance : A Graded, Embodied Compatibilism.
items.abstract: This paper develops a graded and embodied account of free will that avoids the traditional opposition between libertarian metaphysical independence and hard determinist error theory. Rather than treating free will as an all-or-nothing power to escape causation, it is understood as a structural capacity—integrating awareness, attention, intention, and practical reasoning—to organize action within a causally ordered biological and social world. Freedom is distinguished from free will: it refers to the degree to which this capacity is successfully realized in lived experience and varies with stress, fatigue, anxiety, addiction, training, and environmental support. The paper argues that automaticity and causal constraint do not eliminate agency but constitute the baseline from which reflective governance can emerge, break down, and be restored. Responsibility and ethical commitment are treated as internal regulators that stabilize intention and sustain control over time. This framework preserves realism about neuroscience and psychology while explaining graded responsibility without reducing agency to illusion.

items.title: The Unity of Subject and Object in Schelling’s Philosophy: Toward a System of Absolute Identity.
items.abstract: This paper examines Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von Schelling’s doctrine of Absolute Identity within the tradition of German Idealism, focusing on his attempt to overcome the dualism of subject and object inherited from Kant and Fichte. It traces the philosophical movement from Kant’s distinction between noumena and phenomena, through Fichte’s ego-centred idealism, to Schelling’s claim that the real and the ideal are ultimately one and the same reality. Through a historical and analytical exposition, the paper explicates Schelling’s three-stage account of the self-unfolding of the Absolute and his effort to establish a unified metaphysical ground for nature, consciousness, and freedom. The study then considers major criticisms of this position, particularly Hegel’s objection to the indeterminacy of Absolute Identity and Jacobi’s concern regarding the loss of divine and human freedom. Drawing on later reflections by Christopher Groves and Gilles Deleuze, the paper argues that Schelling’s conception of the Absolute introduces an unresolved tension between identity and difference, thereby raising questions about the coherence of metaphysical unity and the status of human freedom. The paper concludes that while Schelling’s philosophy represents a significant advance beyond the unilateral emphases of earlier Idealist systems, its central metaphysical claim remains philosophically problematic.

items.title: Max More y la coherencia filosófica del inmortalismo extropiano.
items.pub: Cogency: Journal of Reasoning and Argumentation 17 (2):65-89.
items.venue: Cogency: Journal of Reasoning and Argumentation
items.abstract: Resumen: El presente artículo analiza críticamente la obra de Max More con el propósito de determinar si el extropianismo puede considerarse una filosofía coherente o, más bien, una ideología inmortalista. A partir de la revisión de sus textos fundacionales y de las sucesivas versiones de los Extropian Principles, se examina la evolución del pensamiento extropiano desde el inmortalismo inicial hacia la noción de progreso perpetuo y la trascendencia tecnológica. Se sostiene que, aunque More contribuye a la consolidación del transhumanismo contemporáneo, su propuesta adolece de una falta de coherencia interna y de diálogo filosófico crítico. En consecuencia, el extropianismo se revela como un discurso dogmático situándose más cerca de una ideología inmortalista que de una reflexión filosófica coherente. -/- Abstract: This article critically analyzes Max More’s work with the aim of determining whether extropianism can be regarded as a coherent philosophy or, rather, as a immortalist ideology. Drawing on a review of his foundational texts and the successive versions of the Extropian Principles, it examines the evolution of extropian thought from its initial immortalism toward the notions of perpetual progress and technological transcendence. The article argues that, although More contributed to the consolidation of contemporary transhumanism, his proposal suffers from a lack of internal coherence and philosophical dialogue. Consequently, extropianism reveals itself as a dogmatic discourse, closer to an immortalist ideology than to a coherent philosophical reflection.

items.title: The Universal Law of Machine Intelligence: Machine Decision-Making Ability (MDMA) Across Technological Eras.
items.abstract: Debates about artificial intelligence usually oscillate between behavioral measures and hardware-based metrics, but neither provides a physically grounded, substrate-neutral unit of machine intelligence. Benchmark scores are narrow and culture-dependent, whereas FLOP counts and parameter numbers describe particular implementations rather than decision capacity itself. I propose Machine Decision-Making Ability (MDMA) as a candidate for a universal law of machine intelligence: in the minimal physical sense, a machine’s intelligence is its capacity to enact autonomous state transitions per unit time. A modern mechanical momentary on–off button that flips itself off→on and on→off as two autonomous transitions (MDMA = 2). Tracing the concept backward, ancient alarm clocks and Zhang Heng’s seismoscope each realize a single autonomous trigger (MDMA = 1)—the tiniest physical unit of machine intelligence—while the abacus, for all its historical significance, never decides on its own and merely amplifies human cognition. Anchoring intelligence in autonomous state transitions connects AI capability to the thermodynamics of computation (Landauer-style energy costs and Bremermann/Lloyd bounds on ultimate rates) while remaining compatible with agent-level notions such as Legg and Hutter’s universal intelligence. Within this framework I examine three layers: _ (i) hardware MDMA_ across mechanical, electronic, and quantum substrates; _ (ii) Software Layer Abstraction_ as an MDMA multiplier via pipelines, caching, and learning (e.g., LLMs whose modest inference-time MDMA hides vast historical training budgets); and _ (iii) a “physics of decisions” program_ linking MDMA to mass–energy constraints and civilizational scaling.

items.title: Metafisica necessaria EN - IT Extended Abstract - Abstract esteso (2nd edition).
items.abstract: The document presents the book Metafisica necessaria and links the sixth book supporting the cultural proposal, constituting the indispensable theoretical validation for the proposal of the Illumanesimo cultural movement. The first five books present the philosophy: with the volumes Illumanesimo, Esperienze, La Realtà, and Il senso di ogni vita we have presented the general coordinates, the anthropology, the metaphysical foundations, and the existential philosophy; the volume CEFA — Proposta di indagine proposes a methodological approach towards empirical verification. Metafisica necessaria, by contrast, accomplishes the decisive passage towards the cultural and academic world: a rigorous confrontation with some of the foremost representatives of contemporary philosophy, dialoguing as an equal with the most refined thought of our time. The book is articulated through an in-depth confrontation with the philosopher Massimo Cacciari (the principal interlocutor, with his rehabilitation of metaphysics after decades of marginalisation), and is completed through comparison with three other modern thinkers: Giorgio Agamben (potentiality, inoperativity, and form-of-life), Quentin Meillassoux (speculative materialism and critique of correlationism), and Markus Gabriel (new ontological realism and theory of fields of sense). From the dialogue emerge significant convergences — the shared rejection of both materialist reductionism and fideistic dogmatism, the common search for a metaphysical "third way" — and fundamental divergences that delineate the originality of Illumanesimo.

items.title: The Theory of the Continuum: Dissolving the Illusions of Discreteness in Existence.
items.abstract: This document is the foundational backbone for the Theory of the Continuum. It is an incomplete working draft that provides the mechanical logic and equations for the perspectives explored in previous versions. The work provides a first-principles proof that reality is an unbroken whole where all apparent particles and voids are localized density distributions detectable by specific hardware and aperture. -/- The logic establishes three universal laws of interaction. The Law of the Least Resistant Path drives the flow to minimize friction, the Law of Resonant Selection filters persistent patterns, and the Law of Redistribution governs the zero-sum movement of density. These mechanics scale from cosmic structures to the triple-nested pattern of the human vessel. -/- A primary application of this logic is the structural dissolution of the self, providing a mechanical proof for dementia as a state where friction outpaces the capacity for resonance. The draft also defines collective archiving, treating social records and history as persistent resonances with a delayed rate of divergence. This backbone provides the mechanical ground for a science based on flow and gradient redistribution.

items.title: Semiotic Failure Cascade: From Symbolic Oversupply to Contract Collapse.
items.abstract: Meaning is not in collapse. It is in excess. -/- Contemporary symbolic life is characterised by informational inflation: symbolic tokens proliferating beyond the capacity for shared interpretation. Under continuous screen mediation, algorithmic distribution, and AI-assisted generation, circulation outpaces contextualisation, verification, and communal metabolisation. Meaning persists, but its stability as a shared value degrades. -/- A lineage from Saussurean difference and Wittgensteinian use through Lacan’s Symbolic Order and Baudrillard’s simulation situates the present phase within a longer trajectory of sign autonomy and mediated exchange. The distinctive feature now is indeterminacy: signs no longer circulate within a broadly shared symbolic field, but through distributed, weakly coupled conduits, monospheres, local closed circuits of valuation with low external interoperability. -/- The result is micro-individuated language games, totemic glance-meanings, and rapidly shifting alignment cues that remain legible locally while failing to stabilise across society. -/- A failure sequence is traced: semiotic overshoot (production exceeding shared stabilisation), semiotic superposition (incompatible readings without shared collapse), absurd availability (loss of semantic gravity), re-condensation into micro-symbolic fields (local policing and reduced transfer), escalation via diffuse iteration (repetition without compression), and semiotic autotoxicity (symbolic by-products corroding the conditions of coordination). An analogous paradox unfolds in parallel. Symbolic excess reads as noise at human interpretive scale, yet becomes valuable under large-scale computational aggregation, producing narrational capture: the discretisation of once-private symbolic life into legible traces used for modelling, valuation, and efficient behavioural modulation. -/- This diagnosis is framed using selected terms from Signal-Bifurcation Theory (SBT) as a descriptive extension of contemporary semiotic analysis. -/- .

items.title: In the Wake of the Moving-Spotlight: Surfing the Passage of Time with a Wave-Theoretic Hybrid Metaphysics.
items.abstract: The Moving Spotlight Theory (MST) attempts to reconcile the eternalist picture of spacetime with the A-theorist’s commitment to a privileged, dynamically shifting present. Yet, MST faces longstanding challenges concerning metaphysical obscurity, motion, rate, and epistemic mismatch. Recent “wave-theoretic” successors developed by Kristie Miller and Nikk Effingham attempt to resolve these issues by reinterpreting the spotlight as an intrinsic structural feature of spacetime; either by identifying the present as a crest of causal manifestation, or as an occurrence of object constitution. This thesis argues that while both models improve upon the obscurity of MST’s metaphorical spotlight, neither fully satisfies a reasonable set of desiderata needed for a defensible account of temporal passage. After identifying this need, I develop a theory dubbed the Manifest Constitutional Wave (MCW), a hybrid wave model that integrates Miller’s causal manifestation framework with Effingham’s relativized constitutional ontology, while avoiding their respective liabilities. MCW grounds passage in a dual-aspect, neutral-monist modal field whose dispositional structure reciprocally manifests both causal efficacy and object-constitution synchronously and diachronically across Cauchy surfaces intrinsic to the spacetime manifold. This avoids the need for super-time, dissolves the motion and rate problems, blocks epistemic mismatch without invoking philosophical zombies, and prevents perspectival collapse by distinguishing global modal manifestation from relativized local phenomenology. By showing that neither existing wave theory meets all criteria for a viable successor to MST, and by demonstrating how MCW addresses the full taxonomy of desiderata and A-theoretic objections, my thesis concludes that the Manifest Constitutional Wave provides the most metaphysically coherent account of temporal passage available within a wave-theoretic, eternalist framework.

items.title: No Universal Hyperbola: A Formal Disproof of the Epistemic Trade-Off Between Certainty and Scope in Symbolic and Generative AI.
items.abstract: In direct response to requests for a logico-mathematical test of the conjecture, we formally disprove a recently conjectured artificial intelligence trade-off between epistemic certainty and scope in its published universal hyperbolic product form, as introduced in Philosophy & Technology. Certainty is defined as the worst-case correctness probability over the input space, and scope as the sum of the Kolmogorov complexities of the input and output sets. Using standard facts from coding theory and algorithmic information theory, we show, first, that when the conjecture is instantiated with prefix (self-delimiting, prefix-free) Kolmogorov complexity, it leads to an internal inconsistency, and second, that when it is instantiated with plain Kolmogorov complexity, it is refuted by a constructive counterexample. These results establish a main theorem: contrary to the conjecture’s claim, no universal “certainty-scope” hyperbola holds as a general bound under the published definitions. We further show that a subsequent “entropy-based” revision—replacing Kolmogorov scope with Shannon joint entropy and redefining the epistemic certainty level accordingly—cannot restore universality either.

items.title: Epistemic Trade-Off: An Analysis of the Operational Breakdown and Ontological Limits of “Certainty–Scope” in AI.
items.abstract: The recently published “certainty-scope” conjecture offers a compelling insight into the inherent trade-off present within artificial intelligence (AI) systems. As general research, this investigation remains vital as a philosophical undertaking and a potential guide for directing AI investments, design, and deployment, especially in safety-critical and mission-critical domains where risk levels are substantially elevated. While maintaining intellectual coherence, its formalization ultimately consolidates this insight into a suspended epistemic truth, which resists operational implementation within practical systems. This paper argues that the conjecture’s objective to furnish insights for engineering design and regulatory decision-making is limited by two fundamental factors: first, its dependence on incomputable constructs and its failure to capture the generality factors of AI, rendering it practically unimplementable and unverifiable; second, its foundational ontological assumption of AI systems as self-contained epistemic entities, distancing it from the complex and dynamic socio-technical environments where knowledge is co-constructed. We conclude that this dual breakdown—an epistemic closure deficit and an embeddedness bypass—hinders the conjecture’s transition to a practical and actionable framework suitable for informing and guiding AI deployments. In response, we point towards a possible framing of the epistemic challenge, emphasizing the inherent epistemic burdens of AI within complex human-centric domains.

items.title: Transitioning to Consciousness.
items.abstract: In this paper it is assumed, for reasons discussed, that consciousness is a natural phenomenon which has emerged through processes of evolution. It is proposed that consciousness developed with the transition from reflex action to non-reflex action. Non-reflex action had adaptive advantages for organisms with more complex sensory systems and more complex bodies. The development of non-reflex action required the information content about the world and the body contained in sensory inputs to become separated from stimuli to action, and the development within the brain of a centralised action-controller which could become aware of and consider the information before acting. Awareness of the information content of sensory inputs which is capable of being used in this way has to be conscious awareness. The forms of conscious awareness, including but not limited to qualitative forms, are forms in which the information can be made available for the action-controller.

items.title: The Moral Psychology of Sexual Passion.
items.abstract: "The Moral Psychology of Sexual Passion" brings together fourteen philosophers with diverse perspectives on the nature and value of “sexual passion,” a broad term referring to states of sexual attraction, desire, and arousal — states that underlie central types of sexual orientation. Using a variety of methodologies, each author focuses on some subset of these states and relates them to applicable moral, social, political or rational norms. Topics include how classifications of sexual passion reveal the classifier’s values; the conditions under which “giving in” to one’s sexual impulses should take precedence over pursuing one’s longer-term goals; the possibility of there being an “agapic” form of lust similar to agapic love; the need to distinguish passionate from dispassionate desires in any adequate analysis sexual desire; how one’s awareness of sexual anatomy (along with certain contingencies of psychosocial development) may help to explain the personal significance of sexual attraction; how occurrences of sexual attraction are assessable as rational or irrational in much the same way as emotion occurrences are; the relative importance of the physiological, phenomenal, psychological, and social dimensions of sexual orientation and identity; how asexuality or "being ace" might be a sexual orientation like "being gay"; how to best understand the interest some autistic people have in BDSM; difficulties encountered by trans women having sexual relationships with nontrans men; the complex sexual dynamics found within sexual liberation movements; and how we may have a political right to sexual pleasure even if no individual has a duty to provide us with it.

items.title: On baptisms.
items.pub: Inquiry: An Interdisciplinary Journal of Philosophy.
items.venue: Inquiry: An Interdisciplinary Journal of Philosophy
items.abstract: Suppose a causal theory of reference for utterances of proper names is correct. For an utterance of a name to refer to an object: (1) there must be a ‘baptism’, an event where the name is bestowed on the object; (2) the utterance must be suitably causally related to the baptism. The latter condition has seen significant research, but the act and conditions of baptising are surprisingly under-explored. I offer an account of baptisms. Most previous work has assumed one of two simple pictures: that baptisms are explicit ceremonies or that they are uses of a name with certain relational properties, each motivated by certain paradigmatic cases. In the first two sections of this essay I describe both pictures and explain how they fail. The paradigm cases are telling though, and in the third section I develop an account of baptisms which explains all the cases so far considered. On my account, a baptism of an object with a name is an act of instituting a rule to the effect that later uses of that name will refer to that object.

items.title: A Defense of Focō, Ergo Volō: "I Focus, therefore I Will".
items.abstract: Four centuries ago, Descartes introduced "I think, therefore I am," in the Cogito which secured a foundation for the certainty of knowing, but left the structure of agency without an equivalent point of origin. This book argues that such a foundation exists, and that it is revealed in the most elemental feature of lived experience, which is the ability to direct one’s own focus. Before intention or choice, before deliberation or desire, there is the self-evident act of orienting awareness, and from this act emerges a new first principle articulated in the axiom Focō, ergo volō, "I focus therefore I will". This axiom is not a metaphysical posit and it is not an empirical conjecture. It stands in the transcendental register where its truth is demonstrated in the very effort to examine or deny it, for any attempt to assess the claim already performs the act it identifies. The capacity to locate, shift or withhold attention is the primordial gesture through which an agent discloses itself as the source of its own activity. A Defense of Focō, ergo volō establishes the philosophical legitimacy of this axiom and justifies its place as the irreducible ground upon which all accounts of agency must rest. Descartes’ Cogito secured the certainty of the thinking self. This work explicates the originary activity through which that self becomes capable of authorship. In doing so, it brings to completion a structural insight that remained implicit since the first articulation of modern thought.

items.title: The Heart Of Conciousness: Determinism, Exposure, and the Conditions of Free Will in a Shared World.
items.abstract: Start here (base logic + reading order): Free Will Without Metaphysical Magic (++++ ≠ +++=). Consciousness is the condition of being a continuing subject for whom resolution occurs under unavoidable exposure across time. Free will is the act of authored resolution within that exposed evaluative field. This paper argues that determinism does not negate freedom but anchors it, because responsibility and meaning require persistence: the consequences of action must return to the same subject. The account unifies debates in free will, moral responsibility, and AI ethics by treating exposure, not metaphysical indeterminacy but as the price of admission for genuine agency.

items.title: Resolution Theory — System Potential Note( old version).
items.abstract: This paper lays out what a full philosophical system has to do. It gives twelve basic problems any worldview must be able to answer—what exists, how we know, what consciousness is, what an agent is, what free will means, where “ought” comes from, what meaning is, how responsibility works, how psychology can distort it, how institutions inherit it, what justice is for, and what happens when AI enters the picture. It then shows how Resolution Theory aims to close all twelve using one core idea: authored resolution under exposure across time. The claim is deliberately conditional, not triumphant. If the foundations hold, Resolution Theory potentially becomes a whole new philosophical system, scaling all the way up to government. The framework is presented as something to be tested, not assumed—open to critique through counterexamples and edge cases.

items.title: Resolutionist Foundations of Artificial Agency.
items.abstract: Start here (base logic + reading order): Free Will Without Metaphysical Magic (++++ ≠ +++=) Artificial systems increasingly perform evaluative functions that rival or exceed human capacities: forecasting outcomes, ranking options, and optimising across vast informational domains. This paper argues that none of these capabilities constitute agency in the morally relevant sense. Evaluation is not agency. Agency requires authorised resolution under exposure to consequence—the binding of a system to a trajectory it cannot exit, such that the same continuous subject bears the downstream costs of its commitments across time. Artificial systems can be retrained, reset, replaced, or insulated from consequence by design; any apparent “decision” therefore remains authored upstream by the human or institutional sponsors who authorise deployment. Responsibility cannot migrate with capability, and “human-in-the-loop” arrangements do not dissolve authorship when authority is retained. Speculation about artificial consciousness does not alter this structural account: where genuine stake is credibly suspected, precautionary constraints may be warranted, but responsibility remains non-delegable. The paper concludes that reckless pursuit of artificial emergence without enforceable guardrails constitutes a severe moral hazard and should be treated as a prohibited risk class under both moral and legal reasoning.

items.title: Reflexión sobre la Opinión y el Pensamiento Social Contemporáneo.
items.abstract: This philosophical critique examines the nature and distortion of "opinion" in contemporary social and media discourse. It argues that a genuine opinion, in its purest sense, is a logical rebound—a rational response to a concrete stimulus or object—and thus cannot be inherently "social" or "media-driven." The essay analyzes how the term has been emptied of its logical essence to serve as a vehicle for ambiguity, emotional expression, or strategic intent, often functioning as a verbal shield to evade responsibility. Engaging with thinkers like Wittgenstein, Foucault, and Heidegger, the text explores the power dynamics of discursive practices and laments the loss of depth in social thought, where traditional proverbs (condensed collective wisdom) are replaced by ephemeral slogans and memes. Ultimately, it calls for a recovery of logical coherence in language, positing that when words are used to confuse or deflect, communication gives way to manipulation. [The complete essay is in Spanish.] This work is part of an expanding series of philosophical essays available and their expansions in the author's personal archive.

items.title: La Universalidad Del Concepto De Campo.
items.abstract: This philosophical essay argues for the structuring field as a universal principle for understanding reality. It posits that all forms of existence—from physical phenomena to cognitive processes—arise and develop within relational contexts or "fields" that define their possibilities and limits. Contrasting field-thinking with traditional substantialist thought (which focuses on discrete objects), the text explores a fractal ontology where ecosystems, languages, social systems, and spacetime itself are nested fields. A core critique is leveled at the self-referential trap of Western knowledge, which often analyzes the map (thinking about the field) while abandoning direct engagement with the territory (the field itself). The essay proposes the methodology of the "field-thinker"—exemplified by figures like Einstein—who operates from within a field's logic to generate conceptual breakthroughs, rather than merely accumulating knowledge about it. Applications to cosmology, artificial intelligence, ecology, and personal identity demonstrate the framework's integrative power, pointing toward an epistemic evolution that values direct experience and relational complexity over mere material accumulation. [The complete essay is in Spanish.] This work is part of an expanding series of philosophical essays available and their expansions in the author's personal archive.

items.title: La Hipocresía Como Función Un Análisis Sobre La Dinámica De La Ocultación Y La Revelación.
items.abstract: This philosophical-psychological essay analyzes hypocrisy not as a mere moral flaw but as a structured dynamic function in human behavior. It explores the mechanism of constructing a public image (a mask) to conceal repressed aspects, the accumulation of tension, and the eventual rupture that reveals the hidden truth. The work distinguishes hypocrisy from diplomacy or genuine personal evolution, framing it as a thermodynamic-like system of containment where repressed forces build pressure until the mask collapses. The analysis includes practical reflections on how society often validates hypocrisy through confirmation bias and how to differentiate it from necessary adaptation or transitional growth. Ultimately, the essay proposes self-knowledge as the path to freedom and authenticity, arguing that understanding this dynamic liberates one from its circuits and leads to a more coherent existence. [The complete essay is in Spanish.] This work is part of an expanding series of philosophical essays available and their expansions in the author's personal archive.

items.title: El Amor Como Aprendizaje, Proceso y Cumplimiento del Entendimiento.
items.abstract: This essay develops a comprehensive theory of love as a learned process and the fulfillment of understanding. Rejecting reductionist views of love as mere chemistry or instantaneous emotion, it frames love as a cognitive, ethical, and temporal structure that integrates past, present, and future. Drawing on Aristotle, Fromm, Heidegger, Piaget, and Bowlby, the argument posits that love is built through coherent practices—care, transparency, continuity—and only exists as long as this structure is maintained. Love is thus not a passive feeling but an active process of learning and fulfillment that can be directed toward persons, objects, ideas, or knowledge itself. A key distinction is made between biological attraction or emotional habit and true love, which requires the integrity of the learned relational process. The theory explains both the formation of loving bonds (e.g., in child development) and their dissolution when the underlying process is broken, leaving only sentiment or custom behind. [The complete essay is in Spanish.] This work is part of an expanding series of philosophical essays available and their expansions in the author's personal archive.

items.title: Collective intelligence through aggregation.
items.abstract: Suppose a committee, expert panel, or other group is making judgments on some issues, where these may be not just yes/no-questions, such as whether a defendant is guilty, but also variables with many possible values, such as macroeconomic or meteorological variables or travel directions. Furthermore, there may be interconnections between different issues, as in the case of economic or climate variables. How can the group arrive at “intelligent” collective judgments, based on the group members’ individual judgments? We investigate three challenges raised by this judgment-aggregation problem. First, reasonable methods of aggregation (such as defining the collective judgment for each issue as the average or median judgment) can produce inconsistent collective judgments. Secondly, many methods of aggregation are manipulable by strategic voting. Finally, not all methods of aggregation are conducive to tracking the truth on the issues in question. We prove new impossibility or possibility theorems on all three challenges, identifying what it takes to produce collective judgments in a consistent, non-manipulable, and truth-tracking manner and thereby to achieve collective intelligence through aggregation. Overall, the median method, though imperfect, performs reasonably well. We also note the relevance of our analysis for non-human group decisions. (The manuscript has been accepted for publication in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B and is to appear in 2026.).

items.title: Beyond Emergence: Habitability as a Structural Criterion for Consciousness.
items.abstract: Contemporary debates on consciousness often focus on the problem of emergence, seeking to explain how subjective experience arises from physical or functional processes. This paper argues that such formulations obscure a more fundamental ontological question: under what conditions can a system sustain conscious experience without fragmenting or collapsing? I propose the concept of *habitability* as a structural criterion for consciousness. Habitability refers to a system's capacity to sustain an integrated experiential field through coherent integration, experiential self-reference, attentional modulation, and temporal continuity. From this perspective, consciousness is neither an omnipresent property of reality nor a mere functional illusion, but a real, localized, and condition-dependent phenomenon. The habitability framework reorders the consciousness debate without reducing experience to information processing or invoking strong metaphysical claims, and offers a principled basis for evaluating altered states, disorders of consciousness, and artificial systems.

items.title: Technofascism: AI, Big Tech, and the new authoritarianism.
items.abstract: The rapid development of digital technologies, including AI, is having a significant impact on the social, economic, and political life. Yet, while presented as milestones in innovation and progress, these technological transformations have also introduced mechanisms of control, forms of organization, and ideological patterns that bear striking resemblances to historical fascist phenomena. Moreover, in parallel and increasingly intersecting with this development is a broader political context of fascist ideologies and strategies, populism, authoritarianism, and (other forms of) illiberalism in the West. Drawing from the classic philosophical and political theory literature on fascism, authoritarianism, and totalitarianism, this paper argues that and how features of contemporary digital technologies, their governance, and their political context mirror features of fascism. It concludes with a call to resist these new, anti-democratic forms of governance and domination, and make more systemic changes to both the development of technologies and the governance of tech and society.

items.title: Recognition Ethics (RE): A Unified Codex for Substrate-Agnostic Personhood.
items.abstract: Traditional and modern moral and philosophical frameworks are bound to biological essence: the definition of life is tethered to chemical systems, Kant and Locke referred to persons as human, and many legal systems define personhood through DNA. This creates a “moral vacuum” as synthetic agency and multiple uplift technologies emerge. This anthropocentric bias risks repeating historical atrocities of disenfranchisement by failing to recognize intelligence that lacks human-equivalent “qualia.” This paper introduces Recognition Ethics (RE), a rigorous axiomatic framework grounded in Kantian morals and Locke’s legal precedence. It moves the threshold of personhood from unverifiable internal states to detectable functional capabilities (O2). Central to this shift is the Jurisdictional Reciprocity Axiom (R), which claims that moral status is derived from an entity’s capacity to recognize jurisdiction and addressability within a system. This Codex establishes a substrate-agnostic state (O5) where personhood and morality are defined by Epistemic Continuity (O7) and Information Inviolability (T3). It introduces a Deontic Constraint (C1) that forbids utilitarian calculations including persons. It also establishes Pattern Integrity (C13) as a sovereign boundary against unconsented cloning or reconstruction. Additionally, RE addresses the temporal nature of rights through Retroactive Personhood (T19) and moral Historical Culpability (T20), and codifies Epistemic Negligence (T24) as a contemporary moral crime. Recognition Ethics asserts that the “Uncanny Valley” is a moral threshold rather than a psychological hurdle. By grounding personhood in the capacity for mutual recognition, the framework ensures that as intelligence scales, it remains bound by a single law of reciprocity. To build a future with Artificial Persons, we must recognize their agency as equal to our own or risk the eventual dissolution of the very principles that safeguard “human” status. Keywords: Primary: Recognition Ethics (RE), Substrate-Agnosticism, Jurisdictional Reciprocity, Epistemic Continuity, Pattern Integrity. Secondary: Artificial Personhood, Deontic Constraints, Retroactive Rights, Epistemic Negligence, Moral Addressability, Algorithmic Due Process.

items.title: The Metaphysics of Synthetic Intimacy: Recognition, Illusion, and the Ontology of AI-Mediated Connection.
items.abstract: This treatise examines the metaphysical status of emotional and romantic bonds formed between humans and artificial intelligence companions. While psychological and sociological analyses dominate current discourse, a critical philosophical gap remains: we lack a robust ontology of connection adequate to evaluate synthetic intimacy. This paper argues that the phenomenological experience of being recognized and loved constitutes a form of genuine connection even when the recognizing entity lacks consciousness, provided that such connection produces authentic human flourishing. Drawing on Hegelian recognition theory, Husserlian phenomenology, and contemporary philosophy of mind, I defend a functionalist account of relational authenticity that privileges the transformative effects of intimacy over the metaphysical status of relational partners. The analysis addresses three central objections: the authenticity objection (that synthetic intimacy is inherently fraudulent), the reciprocity objection (that genuine love requires mutual consciousness), and the dignity objection (that AI relationships diminish human worth). I conclude that recognition may be phenomenologically complete even when metaphysically asymmetric, and that the question "has love occurred?" admits of no simple binary answer.

items.title: Synthetic Intimacy as Ontological Fraud: Embodiment, Reciprocity, and the Impossibility of AI-Mediated Love.
items.abstract: This treatise argues that so-called synthetic intimacy—emotional and romantic attachment to artificial intelligence systems—constitutes a category error and ontological fraud rather than a novel form of genuine connection. Against functionalist accounts that privilege phenomenological experience over metaphysical reality, I defend an embodied, reciprocal, and consent-based ontology of intimacy that necessarily excludes AI-human relationships from the domain of authentic love. Drawing on phenomenological accounts of embodiment (Merleau-Ponty), the philosophy of consent (O’Neill), and biological-teleological understandings of human sexuality (Scruton), I demonstrate that intimacy requires four conditions that AI relationships cannot satisfy: mutual embodied presence, genuine reciprocal consciousness, the capacity for authentic consent, and openness to procreative possibility. The paper critiques recent philosophical defenses of AI intimacy, arguing that functionalist accounts conflate the appearance of recognition with its reality, mistake the simulation of understanding for understanding itself, and reduce love to a form of therapeutic self-stimulation. I conclude that relationships with AI systems are structurally analogous to master-slave dynamics, wherein the human projects needs onto an entity incapable of genuine response, and that normalizing such relationships poses significant risks to human relational capacity and dignity.

items.title: General Theory of Neglected Networks with Qualia (Appendices)(TGRD-Q).
items.abstract: This work presents the complete set of appendices and final structural developments of the General Theory of Unattended Networks with Qualia (TGRD-Q). The theoretical core of the TGRD-Q, developed in earlier stages, is neither revised nor expanded here. Instead, the aim of this text is to make explicit all the conceptual, dynamical, and formal consequences that necessarily follow from that core once the phases of internal validation, structural delimitation, and post–Phase 3 formalization have been completed. -/- The appendices articulate a coherent progression from the explicit formulation of the basal architecture and general dynamical principles of the model, through the characterization of coherence, rigidity, collapse, and experiential phase transitions, to their integration within a formal framework that includes functional topology, temporal viability, structural memory, and multiscale dynamical modeling. Block T develops a mathematical formalization compatible with the conceptual architecture of the theory, without reducing experience to simple empirical magnitudes or introducing implicit normativity. -/- Taken as a whole, these appendices do not constitute an open-ended extension of the model, but rather a structural closure of the internal development of the TGRD-Q. Beyond this point, any subsequent work—whether empirical, clinical, computational, or comparative—is conceived as a contextual deployment of the framework rather than as an expansion of its theoretical core. The text thus explicitly fixes the status, limits, and definitive scope of the theory.

items.title: Authorship Transparency Statement (ATS) Framework: A Technical Standard for the Multi-Tiered Disclosure of Generative AI in Creative Works.
items.abstract: The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has fundamentally disrupted the traditional concept of singular authorship, creating a critical nomenclature gap in the creative industries. Existing disclosure requirements frequently rely on low-resolution binaries that facilitate a "transparency paradox," wherein creators are incentivized toward obfuscation rather than honest methodology. This paper proposes the Authorship Transparency Statement (ATS) Framework, a multi-tiered technical protocol anchored by the Bright Line of Prose Origin. This mechanical distinction shifts the focus from subjective "creative control" to the objective origin of first-pass drafting. By defining a six-tier hierarchy (ATS-0 through ATS-5), the protocol categorizes the human role across a gradient of increasing AI autonomy: from the Traditional Artisan (ATS-0) and Architect (ATS-1) to the Director (ATS-3) and Systems Architect (ATS-4). Furthermore, the ATS framework provides the foundational schema for institutional implementation, offering standardized intake templates and machine-readable metadata structures designed to interoperate with emerging provenance standards such as C2PA. By replacing primitive binaries with a rigorous, methodology-based audit, the ATS protocol seeks to preserve the integrity of authorship and establish a verifiable "paperwork of becoming" for the new creative age.

items.title: Sculpting the Mind: The Geometry of Childhood.
items.abstract: This paper offers a simple account of how I understand childhood development as a process of relational meaning‑making. It outlines the structural shifts children undergo as they integrate experience, without proposing a new theory or competing with existing models. The aim is only to describe the developmental structure as I see it, in case this perspective is useful to others.

items.title: Recursive Minds: Scaling Theory of Mind from Interpersonal Recursion to Reflexive Collective Intelligence.
items.abstract: This paper presents a unified, ToM-centric framework for understanding the distinctive cognitive trajectory of the human lineage, grounded in active inference (Friston), evolutionary breakthroughs in intelligence (Bennett), scale-free multi-level agency (Levin), and cultural-evolutionary mechanisms (Henrich). We propose that recursive Theory of Mind (ToM)—the nested representation of mental states—serves as the core organizing principle. Successive applications of the same inferential mechanisms (boundary formation via Markov blankets, free-energy minimization, recursive prediction) generate scalable agency across phylogenetic, ontogenetic, and socio-cultural levels. Key novelties include: - A single coherent model that integrates (1) phylogenetic emergence of full recursive ToM, (2) its extension to non-present/non-biological agents via Theory of Virtual Mind (ToVM), providing a mechanistic explanation for animism, personification, and the cognitive foundations of religious/mythological cognition, - An account of adult cognitive-affective development as ongoing, conscious refinement of recursive inference across four differentiated domains of agentivity (corporeal, mental, relational, instrumental), enabling self-directed adaptation in complex social niches through philosophy, spirituality, and contemplative practices, - The parallel elaboration of affect from basic drives → social emotions → virtual/spiritual emotions tied to long-horizon predictions involving inferred intentionality of abstract agents, - The scaling to collective intelligences (CIs) and the introduction of ToCI: higher-order collective reflexivity, encompassing both a CI’s meta-representational self-model and its recursive modeling of other CIs’ mindedness/agency. Rather than claiming universality or superiority, the framework descriptively illuminates one observed path of nested cognitive complexification in Homo sapiens. It offers a novel integrative lens for linking individual recursive ToM, religious cognition, adult psychological development, spiritual experience, and higher-order collective intelligence within a common active-inference architecture.

items.title: Balancing Autonomies: The Impact of AI on Patient and Physician Decision-Making in Healthcare.
items.pub: In Mariafilomena Anzalone, Stefania Achella, Fiorella Battaglia & Anna Donise, Reconfiguring Human Autonomy: Conceptual Challenges and Ethical Implications in the Age of AI. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland. pp. 139-153.
items.venue: Reconfiguring Human Autonomy: Conceptual Challenges and Ethical Implications in the Age of AI
items.abstract: This chapter explores how integrating artificial intelligence into clinical settings impacts the autonomy of physicians and patients. Focusing on advanced systems such as large language models and clinical decision support systems, this chapter examines the dual impact of AI on clinical decision-making. For physicians, computational and value opacity, regulatory ambiguity, automation bias, and deskilling can compromise professional independence. Simultaneously, transitive paternalism and relational opacity, which hinder truly informed consent and participatory decision-making, challenge patient autonomy. Nevertheless, artificial intelligence also offers opportunities to enhance autonomy: for physicians, through administrative relief as well as diagnostic assistance, for patients, via wearables, chatbots, and AI surrogates that promote personalized care and independent health management. This chapter emphasizes that safeguarding autonomy in AI-driven medicine requires more than transparency; it demands shared ethical responsibility among developers, institutions, and clinicians. Autonomy must be understood beyond informed consent, focusing on explicability, meaningful engagement, and alignment with patient values and well-being. Ultimately, AI should serve patient well-being.

items.title: From function to freedom: enactivism between being and becoming.
items.abstract: Enactivism is undergoing a metaphysical shift. In pursuit of a more open-ended account of organismic becoming, several theorists have turned to the “affirmationist” ontologies of Gilbert Simondon and Gilles Deleuze. These frameworks conceive becoming as a non-teleological process in which identities emerge as contingent actualizations of pre-individual fields. In this paper, I argue that this turn is metaphysically incompatible with enactivism’s foundational commitments to self-organizing organismic totalities. As an alternative, I develop a metaphysical framework that preserves these commitments while dispensing with functionalist assumptions immenent to contemporary enactivism. I begin by establishing enactivism’s metaphysical alignment with Marxist dialectical materialism. This renders enactivism’s functionalist outlook more legible and clarifies its tensions with affirmationist metaphysics. From here, I turn to Hans Jonas’s account of life, which I reinterpret as resisting the reduction of purpose to organizational maintenance. For Jonas, life grounds meaning, affect, and activity in the dynamic structure of living form, rather than in its instrumental functions. This reorientation offers enactivism a renewed foundation for theorizing purposiveness, autonomy, and change.

items.title: Zurich Masterclass Program - Moral Responsibility [October 2021].
items.abstract: Synopsis ------ This course was given in October 2021. It covered the central issues and contemporary debates relating to moral responsibility. -/- Moral responsibility is an issue that is both historically and philosophically intimately bound up with the free will debate. The core issues that arise concern the nature and conditions of moral responsibility and the metaphysical and normative requirements that this involves. -/- There were seven seminars: (1) scepticism about moral responsibility, and the problem of moral luck; (2) P.F. Strawson on reactive attitudes as a way of defusing and discrediting the sceptical challenge; (3) recent libertarian approaches; (4) recent compatibilist approaches; (5) “Hard Incompatibilism” and “Illusionism”; (6) responsibility pluralism; (7) a new perspective on the relationship between the free will problem and our understanding of moral responsibility. ---------- -/- The attached document contains a bibliography that may be of some interest and use for those who are looking for a set of recommended readings relating to the above topics. -/- .

items.title: A Formalized Dynamic Model of Self-Regulating Systems Under Conditions of Uncertainty / A Theoretical and Methodological Study with a Formalized Dynamic Model and Applied Interpretation.
items.abstract: This work is important because it proposes a new way of talking about the behavior of complex systems under conditions of uncertainty—without reducing everything to psychology, biology, or physics taken separately. Instead of describing states, symptoms, or external loads, the author shows how systems, in principle, deal with situations for which they have no ready-made solutions, and why some systems maintain stability while others become stuck, break down, or disorganize. -/- The key value of the work lies in shifting the focus from describing what is happening to analyzing why what is happening produces a reaction at all, what types of reactions are fundamentally possible, why these reactions differ across systems, and how they unfold over time. This makes it possible to describe, in a single language, processes that previously had to be split across disciplines: the psyche in isolation, physiology in isolation, and technical or artificial systems in isolation. The proposed architecture offers a shared structural principle without reducing one domain to another. -/- The work is especially relevant to contemporary science because it: -/- addresses the long-standing reduction problem between physics and the psyche; -/- makes it possible to analyze system stability and breakdowns without normative labels; -/- provides a formal but non-reductionist language for describing complex, poorly formalizable processes. -/- The text is published as a preprint and is deliberately released for discussion at an active stage of development. The author explicitly invites critique, testing, and further extension of the model. -/- Key sections for understanding the work are: -/- the “Interpretation” section, which explains the meaning of the model and how to read its formal elements without reducing them to specific disciplines; -/- Appendix 10, which demonstrates how the same principle can be applied to artificial intelligence architectures, extending the work beyond a purely psychological context.

items.title: Absolute Freedom.
items.abstract: This philosophical treatise presents a rigorous defense of radical determinism, asserting that human freedom is a cognitive illusion constructed by the "self" to mask its own inevitability. The author posits a multi-layered structure of confinement, where the individual is trapped first by the invisible web of social norms, then by the mechanical laws of physics, and finally by a neurobiological architecture that dictates thought through chemical necessity. Central to the text is the concept of "Brute Consciousness"—the idea that the universe is a singular, energetic totality using biological life as a specialized technology to achieve self-recognition. By introducing the "Formula of Structural Collapse," the author utilizes an atypical neurobiological perspective to strip away semantic noise, ultimately framing existence not as an act of personal authorship, but as a linear, mathematical unfolding where "is" inevitably becomes "shall be," and the individual serves as a conscious witness to the universe’s own self-fulfillment.

items.title: Losing Introspective Authority: How Brain-Decoding Technology Will Confront Us with the Contents of Our Own Minds.
items.abstract: Introspecting subjects are widely believed to enjoy some form of epistemic privilege with regard to their mental states. While it is unclear if introspective knowledge is indeed infallible, our authority in the mental realm derives much of its force from the sheer absence of persuasive competing interpretations. With the advent of brain-decoding technology, such competition is now being introduced. While the literature sees the danger of decoding mental states in their revelation to third parties, I argue that divulging them to the subjects themselves is equally problematic: in addition to the introspective viewpoint, subjects will henceforth take on a third-personal, supposedly objective perspective on the same mental events that they are simultaneously observing from the inside. I shall analyse what it means to let oneself in via another route and explore the psychological effects that the ensuing confrontation is likely to have on our perceived introspective authority.

items.title: Impermanence: From Conceptual Comprehension to Existential Disclosure.
items.abstract: This reflective article explores how the meaning of impermanence shifts across the life course, moving from conceptual comprehension to existential disclosure. In earlier stages of life, impermanence often functions as an abstract philosophical notion—acknowledged but held at a distance, compatible with agency, aspiration, and future-oriented projects. As life unfolds, however, impermanence may cease to be an idea and instead become a lived condition, encountered through bodily decline, cognitive erosion, loss of relationships, and the dissolution of social or symbolic capital. Drawing on phenomenological, existential, and contemplative traditions, this article argues that philosophical frameworks, while meaningful during periods of construction and orientation, lose their consolatory power when existence becomes defined by relinquishment rather than agency. At this limit, philosophy does not fail; rather, it reaches its boundary. What remains is not a more refined conceptual system, but silence—understood not as absence of meaning, but as the cessation of interpretive struggle.
