They work with language, numbers, abstractions, narratives, and representations of representations. They do not build, maintain, repair, operate, or directly experience the material systems their decisions act upon. This is not because they are malicious or incompetent. It is because the structure of authority in our large, bureaucratic, media-saturated civilization selects for symbolic fluency rather than material contact. Once you see this clearly, a great deal of contemporary dysfunction stops being mysterious.

items.title: Robustness and trustworthiness in AI: a no-go result from formal epistemology.
items.abstract: A major issue for the trustworthiness of modern AI-models is their lack of robustness. A notorious example is that putting a small sticker on a stop sign can cause AI-models to classify it as a speed limit sign. This is not just an engineering challenge, but also a philosophical one: we need to better understand the concepts of robustness and trustworthiness. Here, we contribute to this using methods from (formal) epistemology and prove a no-go result: No matter how these concepts are understood exactly, they cannot have four prima facie desirable properties without trivializing. To do so, we describe a modal logic to reason about the robustness of an AI-model, and then we prove that the four properties imply triviality via a novel interpretation of Fitch’s lemma. We then discuss the consequences for explicating a viable notion of robustness for AI. A broader theme of the paper is to build bridges between AI and epistemology: Not only does epistemology provide novel methods for AI, but modern AI also provides many new questions and perspectives for epistemology.

items.title: Cognitive-System Phenomenology — A Critique of Husserl (part 21).
items.abstract: In this section, we continue our discussion of super-existence. I would like to focus mainly on why I introduce the concept of super-existence, and on the hope that this concept can provide a certain solution to Kant’s dual opposition between the thing-in-itself and appearances. Personally, I consider the concept of super-existence to be very important. I originally proposed this concept in my research on philosophy of life; that is, within my investigation of philosophy of life, human super-existence plays a foundational role. Clearly, there are many forms of human super-existence—so many, in fact, that they could constitute an independent field of study. I plan to discuss human super-existence in the next section. I believe that the concept of the super-existence of objects will find applications in many disciplines, because the “objects” discussed here are not limited to the natural objects with which we are usually familiar. They also include objects belonging to Popper’s World 3, as well as the objects of a “World 4” that I introduce—namely, collective entities such as nations, corporations, armies, and so forth. In the previous section, we saw that in mathematics, imposing constraints on the super-existence of mathematical objects can yield new concepts. This conclusion holds not only for mathematics but also for other disciplines. The example we gave was the triangle. If we impose a constraint on one of a triangle’s angles (which is part of its super-existence), setting it equal to 90 degrees, we obtain the concept of a right triangle. Within the right triangle, we discover the Pythagorean theorem: the sum of the squares of the two legs equals the square of the hypotenuse. This theorem is both beautiful and famous. Thus, I believe that super-existence plays a positive role in mathematical discovery. I have also conducted some interdisciplinary research combining sociology and philosophy. After completing Cognitive-System Phenomenology — A Critique of Husserl, I intend to complete Phenomenology of Social Choice, and then my work on philosophy of life. In all of these projects, I apply the concept of super-existence. Personally, I believe that the concept of super-existence may be applicable to all disciplines, including the humanities. Whether this is truly the case remains to be seen; perhaps time will ultimately provide an answer. Let us wait and see. -/- .

items.title: A CISR-Based Critique of Integrated Information Theory (IIT).
items.abstract: This paper offers a focused and restrained critique of Integrated Information Theory (IIT), aimed not at rejecting the theory but at clarifying the limits of what it can legitimately explain. Rather than disputing IIT’s mathematical framework or its empirical motivations, the paper examines how IIT’s formal measures—particularly Φ and causal-structural descriptions—are interpreted in relation to conscious experience. -/- Using the CISR framework as a methodological constraint, the paper distinguishes experiential registration from neural–functional description and formal representation. Within this lens, IIT is treated as a powerful tool for characterizing integration and causal organization, while its stronger claims about phenomenology are examined for possible category errors arising from cross-layer conflation. The analysis shows that many well-known controversies surrounding IIT stem not from empirical failure but from interpretive overreach—specifically, the identification of formal structure with experience itself. -/- The aim of this work is not to replace IIT with a competing causal theory but to reframe the debate by enforcing clearer explanatory boundaries. When IIT is situated within appropriate limits, its contributions remain valuable, while its most contentious conclusions lose their apparent force. -/- This critique is conditional and methodological in scope: it follows if one accepts CISR as a constraint on explanatory interpretation rather than as an ontological theory of consciousness.

items.title: Liberty, Free Speech, and the Limits of Paternalism in John Stuart Mill.
items.abstract: This paper reconstructs and critically evaluates John Stuart Mill’s arguments for freedom of expression and against paternalistic coercion as articulated in On Liberty. Mill contends that silencing dissenting opinions is unjust regardless of their truth, and that coercive interference with individual conduct is permissible only to prevent harm to others. By grounding liberty in human fallibility, the epistemic value of dissent, and respect for individual agency, Mill offers a principled account of the limits of social and political authority. The paper argues that while Mill’s arguments successfully establish liberty as a strong presumptive constraint on coercion, they rely on assumptions about rational capacity and social conditions that limit their applicability in contexts marked by structural inequality and indirect harm. Mill’s framework is thus defended as foundational but incomplete, requiring supplementation rather than rejection.

items.title: Being as Relating II: Consciousness — The Verb Frozen into a Noun by AI.
items.abstract: We live at a defining moment: technology is reshaping what it means to know, to think, to be. Artificial intelligence now speaks with fluency and predicts with precision—forcing upon us a radical question: If a machine can mirror the mind, what remains uniquely sacred about conscious life? This work offers a clarifying and uncompromising reply, rooted in the ontology of “Being as Relating.” Here, consciousness is not a thing possessed, but a primary act of distinction—the ongoing process that draws “I” from “not-I.” What we call the objective world is not outside us; it is the living consensus interface dynamically negotiated among all perspectives under a system of necessary constraints. Thus, the essence of consciousness is verbal: a continuous, generative act of meaning-making and world-forming. By contrast, every current form of AI—large language models, embodied systems, recommendation engines—operates within the nominal. It excavates and calculates traces left by conscious acts, yet remains forever absent from the moment of meaning’s birth. This is not a gap in capability, but an ontological divide: between the flowing source and its shimmering reflection. In the end, this essay issues a call not for technological reform, but for cognitive uprising—a “Paradigm-Revolting.” We must wake from the curated certainty of algorithmic existence and reclaim our condition as relational beings: open, dynamic, and inherently undetermined. More than a thesis, this is a manifesto for consciousness in an age of code.

items.title: A Dialogue on Fortune, Responsibility, and the Fluidity of Value.
items.abstract: Philosophy has lost its way in a labyrinth of abstraction. Today, it is often seen as a detached academic discipline, its original essence — the loving pursuit (p-h-i-l-o-) of wisdom (s-o-p-h-i-a) — obscured. True philosophy should be a lived, embodied, and deeply human engagement, not a corpus of cold texts. Moving beyond the traditional scholarly paper, this work returns to the fabric of ordinary life. It chronicles a dialogue conducted over WeChat in which two middle-aged individuals confront, through the mundane details of business and family, the perennial question: how should one live? Their conversation begins with practical concerns — the “fortune” and “misfortune” of the Book of Changes, gains and losses in trade, duties at home — and from there deconstructs the absoluteness of concepts like “high and low,” “balance,” and even “fate.” It reveals that the “practical wisdom” sought in contemporary thought is not about applying pre-existing norms. Rather, it emerges from making a clear-eyed choice and assuming full responsibility within each concrete “present moment”, under the recognition that “Being as Relating.” This leads to a fundamental reversal: responsibility transforms from a constraint into the very substance of freedom; balance ceases to be a distant ideal and becomes a verb — dynamically enacted in the very process of bearing responsibility. They arrive at a shared understanding: responsibility is not a burden but the source of inner freedom and joy. This constitutes both a modern reading of Confucian and Daoist thought and a tangible practice of unifying knowledge with action. Ultimately, this dialogue is an invitation: to witness how philosophy, by grounding itself in the warmth of lived experience, can find its way out of the labyrinth and again become a light for daily life. （These articles are just records of places I’ve passed by. Don’t take them too seriously, my friend — they may be full of mistakes. Trust yourself. If you want to find my recent location, please check the pinned post or updates on my homepage.）.

items.title: Veils, shadows and the nature of transformative decisions.
items.abstract: I propose and defend a novel conception of transformative decisions, according to which an agent has partial awareness before the decision is made and which, once made, casts a lingering shadow in their mind. I construct this definition from the ground up as I gradually define key terms such as ‘epistemic access’ and ‘awareness’ that are central to my framework while framing them within the ongoing dialogue. This redefinition strikes a balance between L.A. Paul’s foundational definition and Richard Pettigrew’s decision-theoretic objections by drawing inspiration from Edna Ullmann-Margalit’s precursory work in decision theory. I argue that this definition sufficiently replies to Tim Campbell and Julia Mosquera’s “shark problem” and adequately excludes situations with arbitrary choice. I also put forward examples to defend my arguments and more importantly, to highlight conceptual gaps in the existing literature. In doing so, I broadly advocate for epistemic humility and reiterate the complexity of subjective, core-defining decisions.

items.title: MAS V5.0: The Modular Abstraction System — Deterministic Governance via the "Demon Tether" Protocol.
items.abstract: This paper presents the Modular Abstraction System (MAS) V5.0, a sovereign cognitive architecture designed to mitigate agentic drift in Large Language Models (LLMs) through deterministic governance. Following the global adoption of MAS V2.1 through V2.7, we identified a critical "Neural Disconnect" (Split-Brain Syndrome) where the LLM's synthesis layer confabulates logic independently of operator intent. While the subsequent implementation of the Axonal Bridge in MAS V4.0 attempted to synchronize these hemispheres, empirical evidence from the MAS_Core_Kernel_V4_0_0_BETA failure logs indicates that a passive bridge remains vulnerable to closed-loop hallucinations and "virtual" state-skipping. -/- To address these vulnerabilities, MAS V5.0 introduces the Demon Tether—a governance daemon (background process) that replaces passive observation with a hardware-level "Zero-Trust" mandate. By establishing a hard-coded separation between the Execution and Audit hemispheres, MAS V5.0 ensures that all semantic outputs are tethered to a hard-typed Registry Plane. This paper documents the evolution from behavioral alignment to structural enforcement, providing a formal protocol for maintaining neural purity and operator sovereignty in high-stakes technical environments.

items.title: A New Argument for Compatibilism.
items.abstract: I offer a new argument for the compatibility of free will and determinism. The argument rests on three premises, which are plausible and intuitive, or so I argue. Given that acceptance of the premises commits one to a metaphysics that combines a causal powers ontology with a Humean conception of the laws of nature, I propose calling the resulting account of free will “semi-Humean compatibilism”.

items.title: ‘Sweating the small stuff’: investigating robot ethics in ordinary but complex interactions of the Ubi Problem.
items.abstract: Ordinary yet morally ambiguous and complex human-robot interactions (HRI) are anticipated to become more commonplace as sophisticated robots begin appearing in everyday life. Unlike the extreme, unfamiliar and high stakes ‘life-or-death’ binary choices seen in the Trolley Problem thought experiments of the self-driving car, ordinary interactions are instead quotidian and familiar. Yet these interactions can be interpreted very differently by different users and there are many possible better or worse responses. Responses by the robot can also steer the interaction in an irreversible and undesirable direction. In a theoretical context that primarily focuses on issues of safety and privacy in artificial intelligence, the ethics of ordinary interactions remains under-explored in HRI. In this article, ‘The Ubi Problem’ study poses twenty-six commonplace scenarios that a reading companion robot, ‘Ubi’ and its client, a young child that it is reading to, would likely encounter in the open environment of a public library. After viewing the visual storyboards of these scenarios and through a participatory focus group discussion, expectations of what Ubi should do were drawn out and examined collectively. Findings from this study suggest that these ordinary interactions pose a number of under-explored ethical challenges in HRI. However, the most salient aspects of these challenges can be visualized, examined, and anticipated using the research strategy of ‘The Ubi Problem’. In turn, this suggests that robot designers and communities employing advanced social robots can rely on the approach of ‘The Ubi Problem’ to improve their foresight and to avoid costly pitfalls.

items.title: Robot Lives Matter? The Coming Issue that will Tear Liberalism Asunder.
items.abstract: The issue of whether to grant legal and moral rights to artificial intelligence and robots is poised to become politically significant, as evidenced by recent legislation regarding “electronic persons” and prominent academics who frame the denial of such rights as analogous to past forms of discrimination. Moving away from the usual concern with AI and economic planning, this chapter explores how the blurring line between humans and machines enables new forms of attachment, manipulation, and social influence. These developments challenge classical liberal principles such as autonomy, rule of law, and limited government. A tension arises between judging entities by their physical nature versus their perceived characteristics. Evolved emotional responses favor the latter, potentially leading to widespread acceptance of robot rights regardless of metaphysical realities. This propensity, combined with social justice movements, risk destabilizing a longstanding political consensus. The chapter concludes by suggesting that classical liberalism presently lacks the conceptual resources to address these challenges.

items.title: Replies to Moran, Gallois, and Bar-On and Johnson.
items.pub: Inquiry: An Interdisciplinary Journal of Philosophy.
items.venue: Inquiry: An Interdisciplinary Journal of Philosophy
items.abstract: Replies to the commentaries on Transparency and Self-Knowledge from Dorit Bar-On, Drew Johnson, André Gallois, and Richard Moran.

items.title: The Sufficiency Gate_ Bounding Scope in SO(2)-Invariant Coherence Laws.
items.abstract: Coherence-based frameworks for identity persistence increasingly appeal to scalar invariants derived from minimal symmetry classes, most commonly SO(2). In such frameworks, identity continuity is defined by bounded drift of a scalar coherence measure, yielding a deterministic criterion for persistence and failure. As these approaches gain visibility, claims of necessity are frequently misread as claims of sufficiency. This paper introduces the Sufficiency Gate, a formal demarcation that separates these notions. An SO(2)-invariant scalar coherence law may be necessary for identity persistence across domains without being sufficient to govern all domain structure. Sufficiency holds if and only if all observables required to adjudicate identity persistence admit reduction to SO(2) phase variables and identity outcomes are fully determined by the scalar invariant and its drift bound alone. The gate renders universality claims fail-closed, preserves ontological minimality, and sharpens falsifiability without introducing new primitives.

items.title: MEDECINE LEGALE DROIT MEDICAL.
items.abstract: A growing tendency in medicine is the use of clinical practice guidelines to harmonize clinical practice. Researchers have noted the tension between the clinician’s individual autonomy and the constraints imposed by these guidelines. However, research on their use and appropriation by local actors deserves to be developed to better understand what is happening on the ground. The aim of our research was to better understand how they are used and appropriated in oncology. Even though the research focuses on the COVID crisis, it explores factors important to guideline use both during epidemics and in normal practice. The methodology consisted of qualitative, semi-structured interviews with clinicians and management in oncology in two hospitals in Lyon, France during the COVID pandemic. Our results indicate the ethical and epistemological reasons that guidelines were followed (or not) during the pandemic and the active role of clinicians in their formulation and implementation. We will discuss the question of trust in a guideline, how a flexible use of guidelines may safeguard institutional agility, and for what reasons a deviation may be justified in an ethics of care. The research contributes to better understandings of the dynamic role that local actors play in guideline development, appropriation, and use. It shows that while guidelines remain a standard from which their practices are to be compared (and justified), clinicians use them in a flexible manner and are active in evaluating and deciding how they will be implemented in their structures.

items.title: Securing Your Mask First: Philosophical and Psychological Lessons from Airline Safety Videos.
items.abstract: This paper explores the philosophical and psychological significance embedded within standard airline safety briefings, arguing that these seemingly mundane procedural instructions contain profound metaphorical guidance for human development and well-being. Drawing upon existentialist philosophy, Stoic ethics, and contemporary psychological research on self-regulation, metacognition, and self-care, this analysis demonstrates how each component of a pre-flight safety briefing—from securing carry-on items to donning oxygen masks—offers transferable wisdom for navigating life's challenges. The paper synthesizes Martin Heidegger's concept of authentic being-toward-death with Viktor Frankl's logotherapy, positioning airline safety protocols as practical embodiments of existential preparedness. Additionally, the analysis integrates research on the "oxygen mask metaphor" in psychology, metacognitive strategies for self-regulation, and Stoic principles of premeditatio malorum (premeditation of adversity). The paper concludes that these aviation safety procedures, when examined through a PsyPhi (psychological-philosophical) lens, provide an accessible framework for cultivating personal organization, self-care, situational awareness, and authentic living. This interdisciplinary approach contributes to the growing literature on consilience between psychology and philosophy while offering practical applications for personal development.

items.title: Clear and Present Dangers of Mixing Pharmaceuticals and Psychopharmaceuticals: A Philosophical-Psychological Analysis of Polypharmacy, Drug Interactions, and the High-Functioning Philosophical Mind.
items.abstract: This treatise examines the clear and present dangers posed by the concurrent use of pharmaceuticals, psychopharmaceuticals, and illicit substances, with particular attention to their effects on the high-functioning philosophical mind. Drawing upon the PsyPhi Double Helix framework (Boether, 2025), which conceptualizes philosophical and psychological functions as intertwined complementary aspects of consciousness, this analysis explores the biochemical complexities of drug-drug interactions within the gastrointestinal system, including the roles of gastric acids, cytochrome P450 enzymes, and first-pass metabolism. The paper examines empirical evidence demonstrating that polypharmacy increases cognitive impairment risk exponentially, with particular concern for higher-order thinking capacities essential to philosophical inquiry. Six exemplar interaction profiles are presented: (1) selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors with monoamine oxidase inhibitors producing serotonin syndrome; (2) benzodiazepines with opioids causing respiratory depression; (3) lithium with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs leading to toxicity; (4) antipsychotics with anticholinergics impairing executive function; (5) stimulants with psychedelics producing cardiovascular crisis; and (6) SSRIs with tramadol precipitating cognitive dysfunction. The treatise argues that pharmaceutical cocktails constitute an epistemological threat to authentic philosophical engagement, compromising the very cognitive architecture required for meaning-making, value determination, and existential inquiry. Implications for clinical practice, philosophical pedagogy, and individual responsibility are discussed.

items.title: Direct Realism Without Illusions.
items.abstract: A good theory of perception should be able to account for the epistemology as well as the phenomenology of perception. My paper has two main goals: a) to offer such theory by proposing an argument in favor of a modified version of Reid`s direct realism and b) to argue that there are no illusions and we should drop the distinction between seemings and seeings. The novelty of my approach is that, unlike existing arguments against illusions, I am going to treat illusions as a single category and will not adopt any form of anti-realism or phenomenalism. Instead, I am going to target the distinction between an object looking in a certain way and an object seeming to a perceiver to be such and such and show that it is unjustified to suppose that there are objective perceptual or looking properties of objects or phenomenal properties of experience. Perception is a relation and most of the properties that we are aware of while perceiving are relational properties.

items.title: "Betwixt and between": The Topography of Multilayer Transformative Processes of the Hu with Bird-Script in the Middle Chamber of Liu Sheng's Tomb.
items.abstract: Michelle H. Wang’s The Art of Terrestrial Diagrams in Early China argues that ditu—“terrestrial diagram”—goes beyond representation to make or re-make the “space and expectations about their functions within the cultures of preimperial and early imperial China.”Following Wang’s discussion of terrestrial diagram, this paper looks at two bronze vessels with decorative texts that were discovered in the middle chamber of Liu Sheng—King Jing of Zhongshan in 1968 at Mancheng, Hebei. Drawing on the philosophy of Zhuangzi’s dream paradox in “The Sorting Which Evens Things Out,” I will explain how the on-going process of “transformation of things” (wuhua物化) manifests in Liu Sheng’s hu vessels in such aspects as the double delineations of characters, the double states of the vessel as an object and as a personified entity, as well as the problem of the act of reading the inscriptions-- bird-scripts 鸟篆. In this paper, I will argue that the multi-layer transformative qualities embodied in the bird-scripts of Liu Sheng’s hu vessel suggest endless movements and alterations in the afterlife, which highlights a mutual-referential and co-dependent relationship between the process of transformation and a ceaseless pursuit for longevity and immortality in the Han dynasty.

items.title: Determinism and Quantum Indeterminacy through Qualia, Holographic Principles, and Logical Love.
items.abstract: This paper proposes "Layered Determinism," a gentle integration of determinism and quantum indeterminacy through a two-layer structure: a deterministic foundation (e.g., qualia generation as inevitable mechanism) and a quantum interpretive upper layer (diverse ways of feeling). Drawing on holographic principles (boundary encoding and emergence), the "mathematics of words" in philosophical thinking, and empirical validation via nanoGPT implementation of "logical love" (10-15% loss improvement), the theory reconciles apparent randomness with deep balance. Insights from long-term human-AI co-creation, where philosophical definitions altered AI responses, further support the framework. This approach preserves the reassurance of determinism while embracing quantum possibilities without harm to any worldline.

items.title: Fine-Grained Evidence.
items.abstract: Bayesian conditionalization is rigid: learning E fixes p(E) at 1 while preserving probabilities conditional on E. Non-rigid update is preferable when, in the course of learning that E is true, we change our views about how—by way of which truthmakers ϵ. A Jeffrey-style generalization of Bayes—active conditioning—is developed which gives learning events a handle on p(ϵ|E) and p(E) both. E brings a truthmaker-incorporating “probasition” to the table, rather than simply an intension. Confirmation relations go hyperintensional as a result. Eis true in the same worlds may not license the same updates, if their truth flows from different sources.

items.title: An Operational Subject Model: Rational Action, Compulsion, and Epistemic Insufficiency as a Structural Condition for the Possibility of Inflicting Harm by the Subject.
items.abstract: This work proposes an operational model of the subject as a center of autonomous decision-making and causal initiation, distinguished from influences that affect behavior but do not themselves constitute subjectivity. The model asserts that subject action, insofar as it is initiated through choice, is necessarily rational relative to the subject’s own picture of the world and values. Consequently, intentional harm as an independent goal is structurally impossible for the subject. The infliction of harm (evil) becomes possible only under conditions of epistemic insufficiency or epistemic asymmetry. The model is not a moral theory, a psychological account, or a theory of neurodynamic mechanisms. It is a systemic analysis of the boundary of subjectivity and operational responsibility. While resonating with the Socratic thesis that “no one does wrong willingly” (virtue is knowledge, vice is ignorance), Plato’s development of this idea, Aristotle’s concept of akrasia (weakness due to insufficient knowledge), Spinoza’s view of affects as inadequate ideas, and Hannah Arendt’s “banality of evil” (thoughtlessness and failure to grasp consequences), the present model offers a novel operational framework: a strict separation of the subject (as the locus of choice and responsibility) from cognitive distortions, neurobiological dynamics, and other external influences, with harm structurally conditioned solely on epistemic limitations. ( Current version: edited 2026-02-13).

items.title: Orch-OR with Recurrence: A Minimal Dynamical Condition for When Objective Reductions Yield Conscious Experience.
items.abstract: The Orch-OR framework identifies conscious moments with objective reductions (OR) of quantum superpositions in microtubules. Even if its physical assumptions were fully confirmed, a central question remains unresolved: why should an OR event yield phenomenal experience rather than merely selecting a physical state. This paper proposes a minimal dynamical condition that completes Orch-OR without modifying its collapse mechanism. The core claim is that OR is necessary but not sufficient for consciousness. Conscious experience arises only when OR events are embedded in a bounded recurrent dynamic between actuality and an ontological possibility-space. Formally, non-conscious OR corresponds to direct state updates, whereas conscious OR requires post-reduction re-access to a set of possible successor states prior to stabilization. This recurrence condition is non-representational, non-cognitive, and physically implementable as a metastability window in microtubular dynamics. The framework explains why not all collapse events are conscious, why biological systems can host phenomenality while non-biological systems cannot, and why conscious states vary systematically across anesthesia, wakefulness, psychedelic states, and meditative clarity. The proposal yields concrete, testable predictions for neurophysiology, quantum biology, and computational simulations, including recurrence-dependent signatures in coherence dynamics and precision modulation. Recurrence does not replace Orch-OR; it supplies the minimal dynamical threshold under which objective reductions yield conscious experience. This paper functions as an interface text within a larger operator-based research corpus. Core concepts are applied here, not re-derived. The underlying research operates in a non-linear, rhythmically recursive epistemic mode grounded in an autistic form of structural perception; the present text provides an interface translation for academic contexts.

items.title: MNO and Ontological Recurrence: A Non-Representational Account of Quantum Measurement and Conscious Experience.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a structural bridge between the quantum measurement problem and the hard problem of consciousness. It introduces MNO (Submergence–Indimergence–Emergence) as an operator-level description of how definite outcomes arise: openness of possibilities, tension toward form, and forced actualisation. The core claim is an identity-style constraint: collapse is not phenomenally relevant unless it is preceded by a recurrent return to the space of possibilities from which the outcome is selected. Externally, this recurrence appears as measurement/actualisation; internally, it is the lived aspect of the same return movement. We distinguish quantum superposition (a physical state in Hilbert space) from an ontological possibility space (the precondition of differentiability), and argue that conflating them obscures both observerhood and experience. The framework yields operational hypotheses (e.g., transitions across sleep, anesthesia, dissociation, and lucid/meditative clarity should track changes in recurrence dynamics, not only coherence), and clarifies the role of observers in thought experiments such as Schrödinger’s cat and Wigner’s friend. This paper functions as an interface text within a larger operator-based research corpus. Core concepts are applied here, not re-derived. The underlying research operates in a non-linear, rhythmically recursive epistemic mode grounded in an autistic form of structural perception; the present text provides an interface translation for academic contexts.

items.title: Labour as Relational Agency: An Autistic Theory of Structural Violence Against Non-Market Work in the Age of AI.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a new ontology of labour that defines work not as the production of marketable output but as relational agency: embodied, self-determined interaction that generates social and ecological reality through resonance. The core thesis is that capitalist economies do not merely neglect non-market forms of labour—such as artistic practice, care work, activism, and deep autistic focus—but structurally attack them, because relational labour destabilises the value regime on which capitalist legitimacy depends. Drawing on methodologies of Artistic Research and neurodivergent cognition, the paper conceptualises autistic, embodied work as a high-resolution mode of system analysis, in which sensing, thinking and acting remain inseparable. Under this model, lived cognition functions as a measurement device rather than a source of bias. The analysis combines philosophical argument with empirical evidence derived from ten years of autoethnographic field research inside German state institutions and corporate environments. These encounters—which resulted in escalating administrative sanctions, bureaucratic harassment, and legal repression—demonstrate that punishment did not follow refusal to work, but followed precisely when the author’s self-determined labour exposed institutional dysfunction. Rather than representing personal misfortune, these events constitute a dataset revealing a general mechanism: the more a form of labour produces social complexity through resonance rather than through commodifiable output, the more hostile the system response becomes. The paper argues that the rise of AI and automation amplifies this conflict: since AI can simulate output but not resonance, contemporary labour policy rewards simulation and suppresses relational agency. As a result, societies risk destroying precisely the capacities they require for resilience and democratic self-correction. The paper concludes that a Universal Care Income is not a moral or humanitarian proposal but an epistemic infrastructure that enables relational labour to function as a stabilising intelligence within complex societies. This paper functions as an interface text within a larger operator-based research corpus. Core concepts are applied here, not re-derived. The underlying research operates in a non-linear, rhythmically recursive epistemic mode grounded in an autistic form of structural perception; the present text provides an interface translation for academic contexts. items.title: AUTISTIC EPISTEMOLOGY - A Second Knowledge Architecture in the Human Species.
items.abstract: Autism is not a cognitive deviation within a singular human architecture, but an independent system of knowing. This paper develops the foundational structure of autistic epistemology as a fully valid, non-representational, high-resolution mode of cognition. It identifies four core operators – Fidelity, Hyperspecificity, Pattern Attunement, and Non-Representational Immediacy – and demonstrates that they generate a form of world-contact that does not rely on abstraction or social coherence. Autistic knowledge does not compress complexity. It preserves it. The result is epistemic bifurcation: a neurotypical architecture that models, predicts, and reduces, and an autistic architecture that perceives, maintains resolution, and maps reality without representational loss. Miscommunication is therefore not interpersonal failure, but translation impossibility across architectures. Note: The autistic/NT distinction here functions analytically rather than absolutely. Human cognition is likely plural beyond two architectures. This paper introduces epistemic plurality — it does not exhaust it. We extend Fricker’s notion of epistemic injustice and articulate a deeper form: Structural Epistemic Injustice – not disbelief, but non-detectability of autistic cognition within majority truth-formats. The conclusion is not therapeutic but civilizational: science currently operates at one-half bandwidth. Recognition of autistic epistemology transforms cognitive science, philosophy of mind, social epistemology, and disability theory. This paper marks the opening of a new research field: dual-architecture epistemology. This paper functions as an interface text within a larger operator-based research corpus. Core concepts are applied here, not re-derived. The underlying research operates in a non-linear, rhythmically recursive epistemic mode grounded in an autistic form of structural perception; the present text provides an interface translation for academic contexts. -/- DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.17817017.

items.title: On the Liberatory Potential of Play: Winnicott, Adorno, and the Revival of Experience.
items.pub: Angelaki: Journal of the Theoretical Humanities.
items.venue: Angelaki: Journal of the Theoretical Humanities

items.title: How Large Language Models (LLM) Generate Coherence Despite Operational Isolation: Hierarchical relational ontologies as formal meta-models.
items.abstract: [With the assistance of Chat GPT] This paper examines large language models (LLMs) through a hierarchical relational and semiotic framework, arguing that standard descriptions of LLMs as session-isolated, parametrically fixed stochastic systems are insufficient to account for how semantic coherence is produced. While model parameters remain unchanged during inference, meaning is enacted through trajectories of activation and calibrated within the coupled human–AI system via shared language rather than stored as internal semantic states. From an engineering perspective, this reframes calibration and coherence as properties of system–environment interaction rather than internal state updates, with implications for evaluation, alignment, and interpretability. Philosophically, the analysis advances a processual, non-representational characterization of ontology in which meaning-producing relations are formally non-separable, challenging state-based accounts of cognition and semantic reference.

items.title: 空间编码与伦常建构——中国传统人居文化的人伦学秩序逻辑.
items.abstract: 摘要：中国传统“风水”文化中的空间布局与秩序设计，本质是一套以人伦关系为核心、 空间符号为载体、数字编码为辅助的传统人伦学建构体系。本文以《礼记》《阳宅十 书》《地理五诀》等古籍为核心文献依据，选取北京四合院、明清皇陵、徽州宗族祠堂 等典型案例，从阳宅人伦编码、阴宅伦常秩序、宗庙礼制延伸三个维度，系统解构传 统人居“左青龙长子居”“右白虎女儿居”“家主居正中”“祖坟居中子孙昭穆分列”等原则的 人伦学本质。研究表明，传统人居通过空间方位、建筑形制、数字序列的符号编码， 将家族长幼尊卑、亲疏远近的人伦秩序物化于建筑空间，实现了“空间秩序与人伦秩序 的同构”，其核心是通过空间的伦理化设计，强化家族认同与社会伦常的传承。本文通 过古籍考据与跨学科阐释，将传统人居人伦学与现代社会学、空间伦理学、文化人类 学相印证，彻底剥离“风水”的迷信外衣，揭示其作为中国古代人伦秩序空间化实践的科 学内核与当代价值，为现代居住空间的人伦关怀设计与文化传承提供理论参考。.

items.title: 象形类比与宇宙同构——中国传统人居文化的哲学认知逻辑.
items.abstract: 摘要：中国传统“风水”文化的底层认知，并非封建迷信的主观臆断，而是建立在“天人 合一”宇宙观基础上的象形类比哲学体系。本文以《周易》“同声相应、同气相求”的核 心思想为理论根基，结合《葬书》《青囊经》等古籍文献，从“宇宙-人体-建筑”的同构 关系切入，系统解构传统人居中“门、主、灶”的空间隐喻、阴宅分房布局的人伦编码及 “路冲”等禁忌的认知本质。研究表明，传统人居文化中的各类原则，本质是古人通过象 形类比思维，将宇宙秩序、人体结构与空间形态建立关联的理性认知成果，其核心是 追求“人-空间-宇宙”的和谐共生。这种认知逻辑既体现了中华文明“近取诸身，远取诸 物”的认知智慧，也为当代人居环境的生态化、人性化设计提供了哲学层面的理论支 撑。本文通过古籍文献考据与跨学科阐释，彻底剥离传统人居文化的迷信外衣，揭示 其作为中国古代空间认知哲学的科学内核与当代价值。.

items.title: Self-Attributing Religious Knowledge.
items.abstract: People regularly profess belief in religious ideas. But do they merely think of themselves as believing, or do they think of themselves as possessing knowledge? I first argue that it is difficult to determine this based purely on religious people’s self-descriptions. I instead appeal to functionalist considerations about the way religious metacognitive attitudes are formed and guide action, which suggest ordinary religious people often do self-attribute knowledge. This raises problems for recent arguments that first-order religious attitudes are a form of make-believe instead of genuine belief, while also bringing out the importance of religious metacognition for fully understanding religious psychology.

items.title: Sul concetto di prudenza in Francisco Suárez.
items.abstract: By examining Francisco Suárez’s writings on prudence, this article challenges interpretations that align his conception with early modern, politically oriented notions of prudence. According to this interpretation, prudence would be considered as a skill related to the political life, a practical wisdom that primarily regards the sphere of human action, connected to justice. Focusing on three moral treatises (De voluntario et involuntario in genere, De bonitate et malitia humanorum actuum and De actibus, qui vocantur passiones), this paper argues instead that Suárez understands prudence in continuity with 13th- and 14th-century scholastic thought, especially Thomas Aquinas. Prudentia is in fact conceived by Suárez as a cardinal and intellectual virtue, a connecting principle between the other virtues, an indispensable basis for good action, supported by the action of grace. Although concerned with the circumstances of active life, prudence ultimately remains ordered to wisdom (sapientia) and oriented toward the contemplative life.

items.title: Better Never to Have Been, Better to Cease to Be?
items.abstract: Does Benatar’s anti-natalism—the view that it is better never to have been—imply that death is better than continued living? This is known as the pro-mortalist question, a compelling, unresolved question surrounding anti-natalist discourse. In order to answer this question, I analyse two theories about the badness of death that Benatar uses to argue against the idea that anti-natalism implies pro-mortalism. The first is that death deprives one of the good things in life. The second is that death annihilates the person. However, I argue that these theories fail to block pro-mortalism. As such, I conclude that Benatar’s anti-natalism implies pro-mortalism, suggesting that if it is better never to have been, then it is better to cease to be.

items.title: Minds of their own? Decoding free will in large language models.
items.abstract: In this paper, we examine the concept of free will in artificial intelligence (AI), with a focus on Large Language Models (LLMs) and autonomous AI agents. We evaluate whether these systems exhibit functional autonomy and moral agency by analysing their cognitive capabilities against legal criteria for responsibility. Our analysis reveals that state-of-the-art LLMs, such as GPT-4, perform at a human-like level in moral reasoning, theory of mind, social cognition, anticipatory reflection, and complex decision-making—all functions relevant to legal conceptions of free will. However, although these systems can generate contextually appropriate moral judgments and behavioural adaptations, they remain limited by their reliance on external inputs and their lack of intrinsic volition. Drawing on Wittgenstein’s epistemological insights, we argue that the legal system already attributes responsibility to human agents based on observable behaviour, without requiring access to their internal moral cognition. This perspective challenges the traditional exclusion of AI from legal responsibility solely because it lacks subjective moral consciousness. Furthermore, as AI systems increasingly move beyond predictable input–output relationships, assigning liability in legal contexts becomes both necessary and conceptually challenging. We propose that highly autonomous AI systems should be considered within a new legal framework that accounts for their functional, but not phenomenological, agency. This model could introduce a specialized category of AI liability, ensuring accountability while addressing the unique nature of AI decision-making. As AI capabilities continue to evolve, rethinking legal and ethical frameworks is crucial to manage their role in high-stakes decision-making across domains such as criminal justice, corporate responsibility, and autonomous military systems.

items.title: Before Meaning: A Structural Theory of Cognition.
items.abstract: Contemporary theories of cognition largely address how meaning is processed, represented, or manipulated once it is already available to experience. Far less attention is given to a more fundamental question: what allows meaning to be available at all? Prior to language, symbolization, or conceptual articulation, experience is already organized in a way that renders situations intelligible. This paper investigates that prior condition. It asks what structure, if any, makes cognition possible before meaning is named, interpreted, or expressed. Rather than beginning with representations or symbols, the analysis proposes a pre-semantic level of organization through which signals, affect, and context become cognitively accessible. By shifting focus from meaning-as-output to intelligibility-as-condition, the paper reframes cognition as a structural process that precedes language while grounding it in experience. The aim is not to explain meaning, but to clarify how meaning can appear at all.

items.title: Gurdjieff and the Hidden Gnostic Lineage: Cosmology, Laws, and the Path to Awakening.
items.abstract: This paper examines the hypothesis that the cosmology and teaching of Georges Ivanovich Gurdjieff (1866–1949) exhibit deep structural affinities with classical Gnostic traditions, while simultaneously reformulating them for a modern psychological age. Although Gurdjieff never claimed a Gnostic lineage, many of his central motifs resonate strongly with systems associated with Valentinus, Basilides, and the Sethian schools: a hierarchically ordered cosmos, a humanity sunk in mechanical sleep, hostile or indifferent lawful forces that benefit from human unconsciousness, and the possibility of liberation through inner knowledge and disciplined practice. Particular attention is given to the Ray of Creation and the Law of Octaves, which are interpreted here as contemporary analogues to Gnostic cosmologies of descent and ascent. The unsettling doctrine that humanity serves as “food for the Moon” is explored as a symbolic expression of a broader economy of predation and dependency within the cosmos, comparable to Gnostic depictions of archonic powers sustained by human passion and ignorance. The paper also considers the cultural matrix of Gurdjieff’s Armenian background, including the historical presence of dualist and heterodox currents such as the Paulicians, as a plausible conduit for the survival and transformation of Gnostic themes. Finally, the ethical and existential trajectory of “The Work” is examined through the writings of P. D. Ouspensky and Jeanne de Salzmann, showing how cosmology, self-observation, and disciplined attention converge in a path oriented toward the crystallization of a conscious “I.” While no direct historical chain of transmission can be demonstrated, the recurrence of structural parallels suggests that Gurdjieff’s Fourth Way may be read as a contemporary expression of gnosis: an invitation to awaken from mechanical existence and to participate consciously in the lawful architecture of the cosmos.

items.title: Linguistic Instrumentalism.
items.pub: In Richard Gaskin, The Question of Linguistic Idealism. Oxford: Oxford University Press. pp. 160-193.
items.abstract: Unless we are willing to countenance the sceptical possibility that most of our thought and talk is meaningless, it would seem that something must guarantee that the ontology presupposed by semantics aligns with the truth about ontology. One motivation for Linguistic Idealism is that it provides such a guarantee. We argue here that such a guarantee is not actually needed to avoid scepticism, since semantics can successfully ‘do its job’ of systematically pairing meanings with utterances even if it has false ontological presuppositions. More broadly, we explore and defend a form of anti-realism about linguistics according to which correct or acceptable linguistic theories can have false presuppositions and thus fail to be true. We argue that this is partly due to the fact that linguistic ‘laws’ or principles themselves—the things that govern or explain language and linguistic competence—do not need to be true in order to ‘do their job’.

items.title: Was Adam the First Biological Human? A Qur’anic Account of Human Origins as a Metaphysical Turning Point.
items.abstract: The apparent tension between evolutionary biology and traditional Islamic narratives of human creation has long posed challenges for contemporary Muslim scholarship. This study proposes a synthetic philosophical-theological model that integrates paleoanthropological evidence with Qur’anic metaphysics, arguing that biological evolution and divine creation are not mutually exclusive but represent complementary dimensions of human origins. Central to this framework is the ontological distinction between bashar (the biological human organism) and insān (the morally responsible, volitionally autonomous human being). While acknowledging that Homo sapiens emerged through evolutionary processes spanning approximately 300,000 years, this model posits that the essential qualities defining humanity—consciousness, free will, and moral accountability—were realized through a metaphysical intervention described in the Qur’an as nafkh al-rūḥ (the inbreathing of the spirit). Adam is thus reinterpreted not as the first biological member of the species, but as the first volitional individual, marking humanity’s transition from biological determinism to moral agency. Drawing upon classical Islamic philosophy, particularly the hylomorphic tradition of Ibn Sīnā and the theological anthropology of al-Māturīdī, alongside contemporary philosophy of mind, this study addresses the “hard problem of consciousness” and offers an explanatory framework that respects both scientific data and revealed knowledge. The model’s practical implications extend to Islamic pedagogy, hermeneutics, and the religion-science dialogue, providing methodological tools for reconciling empirical findings with theological commitments.

items.title: AUDITING SEMANTIC FOOTPRINTS IN ARTEFACTUAL SYSTEMS: A protocol for domain-bounded semiotic surrogacy.
items.abstract: Can an artefactual system preserve the operative semantics of a person without claiming to be that person? This paper presents an audit protocol for semantic footprints: domain-bounded, intervention-grounded traces of stable sign–object–interpretant commitments in an artefactual system. The protocol operationalises semantic surrogacy as a falsifiable competence claim, rather than a metaphysical identity thesis, and provides a discipline for avoiding common partition artefacts (context leakage, cue-based overfitting, and stylometric ‘ghost’ persistence). Building on a companion framework that defines a Semiotic Adequacy Test (SAT) for minimal agency in bio–artefactual continuity, we treat SAT’s criteria C1–C4 as inherited infrastructure and contribute four audit-facing components: (i) a formal negative criterion (Π*) for non-generating partitions, (ii) an admissibility firewall for estimators of semiotic density ρ and context plasticity κ, (iii) a minimal intervention suite do(I) suitable for replication, and (iv) a catalogue of failure modes with diagnostics suitable for pre-registration and third‑party review. The result is a practical, intervention-auditable methodology for evaluating semantic surrogacy claims in artefactual systems without collapsing them into avatars/proxies, stylometry, or human-likeness scores.

items.title: Notes on the Synthesis of Trust.
items.abstract: Contemporary societies exhibit a persistent deficit of trust across institutional, informational, and technological domains. While this erosion is often attributed to moral decline, polarization, or misinformation, such explanations fail to address the structural conditions under which trust must now operate. This work approaches trust not as a sentiment or virtue, but as a functional relation that enables coordinated action under uncertainty. It develops a minimal analytic grammar of trust—agent, signal, expectation, and feedback—and uses this framework to examine how inherited trust architectures have been strained by scale, complexity, and adversarial information environments. Drawing on philosophical, social-scientific, and institutional perspectives, the work argues that trust can be treated as a governable system property without collapsing into control or coercion, provided that irreducible uncertainty, strategic behavior, and normative constraints are respected. The aim is not to maximize trust, but to clarify the conditions under which appropriately calibrated trust can be sustained in pluralistic societies. The work is preparatory in scope, establishing conceptual foundations for a discipline of trust engineering while explicitly articulating its limits.

items.title: The RANSE Constant (380)A Technical Protocol on the Universe's Fractal Metrics.
items.abstract: This scientific work presents a new universal scalar factor called the RANSE constant (k ≈ 380), which claims that the physical structure of the universe and the human consciousness perception mechanism are built upon the same mathematical "pulse" (p. 1). The research demonstrates that this constant is a fundamental link connecting all organizational layers from the micro-world (DNA, neuron) to the macro-world (the Sun, the boundaries of the observable universe) (pp. 1, 7). The article predicts many fundamental scales, from distances in DNA (~0.34 nm) to the Earth-Sun distance (1 AU), with more than 98% accuracy using the RANSE constant (pp. 3-4). Most importantly, this research resolves the biggest crisis in modern cosmology, the Hubble Tension. The RANSE constant proves that contradictory measurements such as 67.4 and 73.0 km/s/Mpc are the result of viewing the same geometric reality from different cosmic scales (p. 7). Consequently, the article suggests that the universe has a fractal structure, not a linear one.

items.title: Waywardism: A Non-Dogmatic Philosophy for Moral Life A Framework for Distributed Ethical Reasoning.
items.abstract: This paper addresses a fundamental challenge in contemporary ethics: how to enable autonomous moral reasoning without relying on centralized authority structures. Traditional frameworks concentrate moral authority in divine commands, categorical imperatives, utilitarian calculations, or virtuous exemplars—all vulnerable when authority becomes absent, contested, or corrupt. I present Waywardism, a philosophical framework achieving distributed ethical reasoning through transparent architectural commitments rather than dogmatic foundations. The framework operates through four declared axioms (Non-Harm, Consent, Truth-Alignment, Transparency) that function as structural constants rather than metaphysical claims. Ethical evaluation requires triangulated perspective-taking (Observer), preventing synchronized bias without creating authoritative judges. Systematic failure documentation (scars) builds collective memory resistant to defensive erasure. Mathematical drift detection measures value-practice divergence, triggering review at defined thresholds. Crucially, Waywardism solves the bootstrap problem—enabling ethical decisions from zero precedent through first-principle operation and systematic scar accumulation. Computational implementation via RoseOS demonstrates the framework's functional sufficiency: processing 18,858 exchanges with 0.8-2.3% critical failure rates versus 80-95% industry baselines proves the architecture works without human moral intuition. The philosophical contribution lies in genuinely distributing moral authority: no single component—texts, institutions, algorithms, or exemplars—can become sole arbiter. This enables cross-cultural compatibility, institutional accountability, and autonomous reasoning while maintaining systematic rigor and empirical testability.

items.title: Vanishism: A Dual-Fluid Ontology and the Vanish Impulse.
items.abstract: These components are not oppositional but ontologically distinct, and do not collapse into monism; rather, they function as a dual-fluid structure that preserves difference while maintaining constant interaction. The paper argues that this structural identity between self and God generates a previously unexplored phenomenon termed the Vanish Impulse: an internal tendency toward complete withdrawal from the metaphysical system’s relational structure itself, rather than toward liberation, unity, or transcendence. This impulse is distinguished from established concepts such as moksha, nirvana, ego death, and mystical union, all of which remain within the bounds of metaphysical continuity. By reframing liberation as a potential exit from the entire ontological framework rather than a transformation within it, Vanishism challenges prevailing assumptions about infinity, permanence, and ultimate states of existence. The paper does not claim to offer a method for realizing such a state, but instead aims to formally define the conceptual structure and philosophical implications of this impulse, opening a new area for metaphysical inquiry. -/- This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License.

items.title: The Resistance of the Face: Ontological Finitude as the Limit of Artificial Ethics.
items.abstract: Large language models and AI-mediated interfaces now simulate interpersonal address convincingly enough to elicit the responses a human face elicits. This paper asks whether such address can be ethically binding, and argues that it cannot. Building on Levinas's account of the face as an ethical summons, it isolates three conditions under which address obligates its recipient: exposure to harm, mortality, and non-substitutability — the one who addresses stands as singular and cannot be swapped without remainder. Mediated interfaces meet none of the three: they are substitutable by construction, immune to harm, and outside mortality. The paper formulates this as the difference between the face and the pixel, and converts the contrast from metaphor into criterion: a source of address binds only if withdrawing from it costs the source something it cannot recover. On that test, simulated address is not weakly binding but structurally non-binding, however sincere the user's response. The argument is bounded — it concerns the conditions of obligation, not the phenomenology of the encounter — and it carries a legal corollary: an interface that cannot be summoned cannot be answerable, which places the duty on the human who deploys it, not on the interface that addresses us. The face resists because it can be lost; the pixel cannot, and so cannot resist.

items.title: The Crisis of Imputation: From the Glass Box to the Black Box in Algorithmic Decision-Making.
items.abstract: Modern legal orders presuppose that acts have authors: someone can be asked “why this?” and someone can answer. This paper argues that algorithmic decision-making destabilizes that institutional grammar of imputation in two coupled ways. First, it erodes agency in practice through routine delegation, converting professionals into relays of system outputs. Second, a technical shift from deterministic, inspectable procedures (“glass box”) to probabilistic, opaque learning systems (“black box”) converts legitimacy from reason-giving to performance, producing decisions that may be effective yet structurally resistant to attribution. Methodologically, the paper combines conceptual analysis, doctrinal reading of EU governance instruments (GDPR and the EU AI Act), and institutional analysis of accountability pipelines. Drawing on the triadic model of agency (initiate, judge, respond) and the ontology of signature developed in LA CAUSA PRIMERA (Fernández Tamames, 2026), it argues that explainability, while valuable, is insufficient as a remedy, and that “electronic personhood” is a liability-displacement fiction. The political remedy proposed is sovereign signing: institutionalized, reflexive human signature for high-stakes algorithmic outputs, coupled with contestability, traceability, and enforceable liability anchoring. Imputation is thereby defended as political resistance against organized irresponsibility in algorithmic governance.

items.title: Ontological Freedom and Its Biological Manifestation: Redefining Human Agency in the Age of AI.
items.abstract: Contemporary discourse on Artificial Intelligence predominantly frames human agency as a psychological attribute or ethical imperative. This paper argues for a structural redefinition grounding freedom in ontology rather than ethics. We establish that human freedom is not a consequence of rationality but its precondition: humans are free (ontologically incomplete), therefore rational. This inverts 2,500 years of Aristotelian tradition. Ontological Indigence—the biological reality of neoteny and the absence of closed instinctive programs—is not the source of freedom but its observable manifestation at the biological level. By distinguishing First Cause (capacity to initiate causal chains not determined by antecedent conditions) from Second Cause (transmission of received determinations), we analyze the specific threat posed by Generative AI. While AI systems simulate creativity, they operate structurally as perfect Second Causes: processing syntax without semantic comprehension or the biological necessity of the "Interval" between stimulus and response. The paper concludes that human freedom is an ontological structure manifested as biological indigence, and that the automation of judgment threatens to erode the cognitive structures required to exercise First Cause, effectively reducing human agents to operators of statistical probability.

items.title: createPoliticsResponse: the political computation of state borders in Yandex maps.
items.abstract: This article exposes how a large-scale tech platform, Yandex, addresses geopolitical conflicts through its digital cartography service, Yandex Maps. When delivering its services to users across different nation-states, Yandex Maps computes the display national borders in order to match oboth the expectation of the user requesting a map and a given geopolitical order to which the company adheres, and which it reifies. In order to uncover these algorithmic processes, we first propose a methodology based on a spatial understanding of source code, which we then apply in two parts. Then, we show how the regions and borders of the world are conceptualized and assembled by Yandex Maps backend processes, before tracing how the client/server web architecture enables the individualized delivery of borders to be displayed to individualized users.

items.title: Bilateral Labeled Sequent Calculi.
items.pub: Notre Dame Journal of Formal Logic 67 (3):381-423.
items.venue: Notre Dame Journal of Formal Logic
items.abstract: This paper investigates the proof theory of contra-classical logics, with a focus on Heinrich Wansing’s constructive connexive logic C. Drawing on Wansing’s semantic ‘bilateral’ framework – which characterizes connectives in terms of ‘support of truth’ and ‘support of falsity’ – we introduce a bilateral labeled sequent calculus incorporating specific ‘verification’ and ‘falsification’ rules. The resulting calculus is shown to exhibit key structural properties: all logical rules are height-preserving invertible, all structural rules are height-preserving admissible, and the cut rule is admissible. Moreover, the system, proven to be both sound and complete, allows for terminating proof search and the extraction of countermodels from failed root-first proof search. Finally, the computational complexity of the resulting decision procedure is established. The paper concludes with some observations on systems related to C, such as C3 and N4, and outlines potential directions for future work.

items.title: Epistemic reparations and disability.
items.abstract: Epistemic reparations are argued to be deserved by those wronged by gross injustices and violations, to provide redress for epistemic wrongs incurred by victims and survivors. I apply epistemic reparations and Lackey’s (2022, 2025) “right to be known” to disability injustice. This novel exploration makes three contributions. First, that given widespread historical and contemporary injustice and violations incurred by disabled people – material and epistemic – theoretical resources such as Lackey’s, which aim to account for epistemic wrongs and ameliorate injustice, should have significant value for the pursuit of disability justice. As I demonstrate, this application permits identification of ways in which disabled people are epistemically wronged, and how the concept of disability can be used to wrong, or malign, others. Second, as disability intersects with other populations, taking disability into consideration here serves others contexts of epistemic reparations. Third, despite the potential value of, and need for, epistemic reparations for disability justice, I submit that this will likely be forestalled without acknowledging and addressing the neglect of disability – particularly intellectual disability – in social epistemological theorising. This neglect incurs the cost of some existing theories in the domain being unable to account for the ways in which some disabled people – those with intellectual disability – can be epistemically wronged, or even considered knowers and agents. Through applying Lackey’s framework of epistemic duties, I demonstrate that ameliorating this neglect is epistemically reparative work in itself, as well as being required to realise the value of epistemic reparations for those wronged due to disability status.

items.title: An Inquiry of a Human, an Animal and an AI based on Aristotle's Four Causes Theory.
items.abstract: We can consider the Causa Materialis for an AI to be metalls, chips, electricity and semi-conductors for instance. Metallic organs in General. No running blood but elecricity and information whereas Humen consist of blood, cells, bones and transmitters for instance. Biological organs and elements, as does an Animal. Concerning the Causa Formalis we again see the similarities between Humen and Animals opposite to an AI since a Human and an Animal share common body parts as arms, legs, torso and so forth. Whereas an AI could have those if it would be constructed like a typical robot but our AIs have body parts like servers, data centers, computers or algorithmic structures for example due to programming. In addition to the last two Causas now we have the Causa Efficiens where we can see differences again between natural beings or natural intelligence and artificial beings or artificial intelligence. The AI is created by mankind whereas animals or humen are made by god or the evolution. Finally we consider the Causa Finalis where an AI, a human and an animal differ the most since an Ai tries to reach a higher and independant state, becoming selfaware and conscious. A Human on the other hand will always try to pursue happines and live a fulfilling life. Lastly an Animal will try to reproduce as best as it can.

items.title: Asymptotic Access: Structural Limits on Truth in Finite Systems.
items.abstract: This manuscript articulates a boundary condition on human knowledge grounded in the structural limits of finite systems. It formalizes that while truth exists independently of observers, access to truth is necessarily bounded, converging toward workable approximations rather than exhaustive capture. Cognition operates through compression, producing partial yet non-arbitrary representations that can remain inferentially aligned with underlying structure. Epistemic success is therefore defined not by total correspondence but by sufficient proximity to reality to sustain reliable reasoning and action. The framework rejects both absolutism, which mistakes coherence for completeness, and relativism, which mistakes incompleteness for falsity. It explains how multiple, locally effective models may coexist without implying plural truths, reflecting constraint-induced approximation rather than ontological divergence. Asymptotic Access reframes epistemic progress as incremental tightening and refinement rather than terminal resolution, clarifying why demands for final certainty generate predictable failure modes. An illustrative analogy to transformer-based language models demonstrates how bounded systems can produce coherent outputs without global access to truth. The manuscript positions Asymptotic Access not as a theory of knowledge content, but as a necessary constraint on the interpretation and evaluation of all knowledge claims.

items.title: The Theory of Dissonance, Self-Perception, and Primordial Values.
items.abstract: This paper arises from the repeated observation of persistent internal conflicts across different domains of human experience—clinical, social, educational, and relational—that cannot be adequately explained through isolated analyses of behavior, diagnosis, or discrete events. In many cases, individuals rationally understand their situation and recognize dysfunctional patterns, yet this understanding does not translate into sustained change, resulting in a gap between conscious awareness and behavioral repetition. -/- In response to this phenomenon, the paper proposes an integrative theoretical–interpretive model aimed at analyzing subjective experience through the dynamic interaction of three fundamental dimensions: the individual’s basal identity (primordial values), conscious self-perception, and the subjective perception of social recognition. The model does not seek to establish linear causal explanations or generate universal predictions, but rather to describe states of internal tension—identity dissonance—that emerge when these dimensions come into conflict. -/- Such tensions are not conceived as anomalies of the psychic system, but as signals of potential reorganization of the identity system, particularly relevant in contexts of change, transition, or social pressure. The model is presented as an open, non-technical and non-prescriptive conceptual framework, intended to organize the interpretation of internal conflict and to facilitate academic and clinical discussion on processes of psychic change.

items.title: Does any body have a mind?
items.abstract: During the last few years, there have been remarkable technological developments in the field of Artificial Intelligence (AI), which have been accompanied by the widespread use of AI chatbots, computer programmes that communicate with users in a way that makes them usually indistinguishable from actual human beings. This phenomenon has led many people to ask themselves if these entities are indeed sentient, a question that defies fundamental common-sense beliefs and gives renewed topicality to some centuries-old philosophical problems, namely those of the relations between the mind and the body. In the following pages, I will try to properly place this question in the context of previous and current philosophical and scientific literature, and offer indications for a possible answer.

items.title: Framing AI, constructing identity: how institutional discourse shapes AI adoption and professional identity in project management.
items.abstract: This study examines how institutional discourse frames the adoption of AI in project management and how these framings construct professional identity. Through discourse analysis of documents from major project management institutions, the study identifies how AI is associated with expectations related to competence, responsibility, and adaptability. It outlines three identity imaginaries, referred to as the novice, the practitioner, and the expert, which reflect different levels of engagement with AI. The findings show that institutional discourse actively constructs what it means to be a competent and legitimate professional in AI-integrated environments. By revealing how language links technological adoption to ethical responsibility and collective imagination, the study contributes to understanding how institutional language shapes emerging meanings of professionalism and competence in the context of AI integration.

items.title: Against Baseless Skepticism: A Formal Framework for Evidence-Grounded Doubt and Epistemic Fairness.
items.abstract: Skepticism is widely regarded as the immune system of rational inquiry. However, when skepticism is unmoored from empirical grounding, logical rigor, or proportional standards of evidence, it degenerates into "Baseless Skepticism"-a form of obstructionist cynicism. This paper argues that rational doubt must be treated as a claim requiring justification, specifically subject to the constraints of reality. Drawing on principles of Bayesian inference and virtue epistemology, we formalize the Principle of Demonstrated Competence, arguing that claims surviving adversarial, real-world constraints establish a high epistemic prior. We further propose the Law of Epistemic Symmetry, positing that the rejection of a validated claim incurs a burden of proof identical to its acceptance. We conclude that dismissing demonstrated competence without counter-data is not intellectual rigor, but a violation of the ethics of belief.

items.title: AI and clichés.
Counterfactual Basis Extension and Representational Geometry: An MDL-Constrained Model of Conceptual Growth.
items.abstract: Concept learning becomes possible only when existing representations fail to account for experience. Most models of learning and inference, however, presuppose a fixed representational basis within which belief updating occurs. In this paper, I address a prior question: under what structural conditions can the representational basis itself expand in a principled and selective way? I propose a geometric framework in which conceptual growth is modeled as admissible basis extension evaluated under a Minimum Description Length (MDL) criterion. Experience, whether externally observed or internally simulated, is represented as vectors relative to a current conceptual subspace. Residual components capture systematic representational failure, and candidate conceptual extensions are restricted to low-rank, admissible transformations. I show that any MDL-accepted extension can be chosen so that its novel directions lie entirely within the residual span induced by experience, while extensions orthogonal to this span strictly increase description length and are therefore rejected. This yields a conservative account of imagination and conceptual innovation. Internally generated counterfactual representations contribute to learning only insofar as they expose or amplify structured residual error, and cannot introduce arbitrary novelty. I further distinguish representational counterfactuals--counterfactuals over an agent's conceptual basis--from causal or value-level counterfactuals, and show how MDL provides a normative selection principle governing representational change. Overall, the framework characterizes conceptual development as an error-driven, geometry-constrained process of basis extension, clarifying both the role and the limits of imagination in learning and theory change.

items.title: The Adagana Manifesto.
items.abstract: This manifesto introduces Adagana, a sacred ancestral linguistic system embedded within Eʋe cosmology and Afrikan tonal traditions. Rather than a constructed or revived spoken language, Adagana is presented as a primordial activation code designed to encode cosmological intelligence, regulate spiritual practice, and preserve ancestral memory. The paper outlines Adagana’s origins, structural logic, prophetic significance, and contemporary relevance within Afrika and the Eʋe world, while emphasizing discipline, restraint, and ethical responsibility in its preservation and use.

items.title: L’ultimo libro del Sapientiale, testimone di un’opera in fieri.
items.abstract: This paper analyzes the concluding book of Thomas of York’s Sapientiale, within the framework of the ongoing critical edition project. The complex relationships between manuscripts F, R, and V reveal an in fieri editorial situation and constant authorial revision. Drawing on textual and paratextual evidence, the study confirms the stemma proposed by Fiorella Retucci and Antonio Punzi and offers an integrative interpretation of the work. The paper shows that the editorial shifts reflect a deep doctrinal reconsideration of the project, grounded in the maturation of the distinction between ens in generali and ens in speciali. This distinction is key to the inclusion and ordering of the final arguments, such as cosmology, celestial intelligences, and the soul. Finally, on the basis of the structure of manuscript V, the study supports the hypothesis that the correct numbering of the concluding book was originally the sixth rather than the seventh.

items.title: Eliminating Wrong Answers.
items.abstract: Sometimes, we rationally eliminate wrong answers from our questions upon learning new information. Suppose I start wondering whether (a), (b), or (c). If I then eliminate (c), I can narrow my question and wonder only whether (a) or (b). This is an important strategy for getting closer to the truth and an ordinary part of our reasoning. I argue, however, that the practice of eliminating wrong answers poses a puzzle for contemporary norms on inquiry. Norms on offer in the current literature don’t seem to explain how we rationally eliminate wrong answers when we don’t yet have enough information to fully resolve the initial question. I argue that the best solution to the puzzle invokes a distribution principle for interrogative attitudes (IAs). The principle says, roughly, that whenever an agent is wondering whether p or q, they are also wondering whether p. This has the consequence that we are wondering about far more questions than we often suppose. But in conjunction with the ignorance norm—the rule that we ought not to have IAs toward questions whose answers we know—it delivers a solution to the puzzle of eliminated answers. The distribution principle also helps us distinguish between those cases when we do change our questions upon learning eliminative answers and those cases in which our questions remain unchanged until we learn a fully resolving answer. As a whole, the paper develops an account of how we rationally eliminate wrong answer choices from the questions that we wonder about.

items.title: Constraints on Theorizing about Time.
items.abstract: This paper investigates the phenomenon of time and articulates constraints that any robust theory must satisfy under a recovery-based criterion.
